units.title: Scientific Inquiry, Measurement & Vectors
units.anchoring_phenomenon: A hiker uses a GPS that says they walked 12 km, but they are only 5 km from where they started. How can the distance traveled be so different from how far they actually moved?
essential_questions: How do scientists design experiments that produce reliable and valid results?
Why does precision in measurement matter in physics?
How can we represent quantities that have both magnitude and direction?
units.crse_theme: Students explore measurement systems from diverse cultures — Egyptian cubits, Chinese chi, Yoruba counting systems — and examine how Lewis Howard Latimer's precise technical drawings were essential to patenting the electric light bulb, connecting precision and cultural contribution.

formative: Exit tickets on significant figures and percent error
summative: Measurement and Graphical Analysis Lab Practical

investigations: Investigation 1: Graphical Analysis of Motion Data

lessons.title: The Scientific Method and Experimental Design
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can identify the components of a controlled experiment and design a procedure that tests a single independent variable.
lessons.circle_prompt: Think of a question you have wondered about the physical world — why is the sky blue, how do planes fly, why do we slip on ice. Share your question with the circle.
lessons.do_now: A student wants to test whether heavier balls roll faster down a ramp. List two variables they must keep constant and explain why.
materials: Balls of varying mass and size (steel, rubber, marble, ping-pong)

engage.description: Show a 60-second clip of a Rube Goldberg machine. Ask: How many cause-and-effect relationships can you spot? Could you predict the outcome if one piece changed? Introduce the idea that physics is about finding predictable relationships through careful experimentation.

explore.description: Groups receive a ramp, three different balls, and a meter stick. Challenge: Which ball reaches the bottom fastest? Students design their own procedure, run three trials, and record data. No formal instructions given — students discover the need for controls organically.

explain.description: Class debriefs: Which groups got consistent results? Which did not? Introduce formal vocabulary: independent variable, dependent variable, controlled variables, hypothesis, trial, reproducibility. Students label their experiment using these terms on the graphic organizer.

elaborate.description: Students redesign their experiment with proper controls. They write a hypothesis in if/then/because format and identify at least three controlled variables. Groups swap procedures and check for clarity and completeness.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: Given a scenario about testing whether ramp angle affects ball speed, students identify the independent variable, dependent variable, and two necessary controls.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a fill-in-the-blank experimental design template with sentence starters for hypothesis, variables, and procedure steps.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the experimental design activity using the graphic organizer with guided prompts.
differentiation.advanced: Design a second experiment that tests a different variable (ramp surface texture) and predict how results would compare. Include a discussion of potential sources of systematic error.
differentiation.ell: Provide a bilingual vocabulary list (Spanish/English) for experimental design terms; use labeled diagrams of the experimental setup; allow verbal explanations during the Elaborate phase.
differentiation.iep: Reduce the number of required controlled variables to two; provide a pre-labeled diagram of the setup; allow extra time for the exit ticket with a word bank.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how Jagadish Chandra Bose, an Indian physicist, designed rigorous experiments on radio waves in the 1890s but was initially denied credit by Western scientists — highlighting how bias in science can affect whose discoveries are recognized.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'controlled experiment': A controlled experiment changes only one variable because___. An experiment may have many trials, but___. The student kept the ramp angle the same for every test, so___.

vocabulary.definition: The variable deliberately changed by the experimenter to test its effect
The variable that is measured or observed in response to changes in the independent variable
A variable that is kept constant throughout the experiment to ensure a fair test
A testable prediction about the relationship between variables, often written in if/then/because format
A single repetition of an experiment; multiple trials improve reliability
The ability of an experiment to produce consistent results when repeated by the same or different researchers

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: What Is Physics? — The Study of Matter, Energy, and Their Interactions
Section 2: Steps of the Scientific Method
Section 3: Variables — Independent, Dependent, and Controlled
Section 4: Writing a Testable Hypothesis
Section 5: Designing a Controlled Experiment

cer.phenomenon: Two students test whether ball mass affects rolling speed on a ramp. Student A uses the same ramp angle and surface for all balls but releases them from different heights. Student B uses the same ramp angle, surface, and release height for all balls. Student A concludes that heavier balls roll faster. Student B finds no significant difference.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the experimental designs described, I claim that Student ___'s results are more reliable because...
cer.evidence_source: Compare the controlled variables in each student's procedure and identify which variables were and were not held constant.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because when a controlled variable is not held constant, it introduces ___, which means the results cannot be attributed solely to the independent variable.

lessons.title: Measurement, SI Units, and Significant Figures
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can take measurements using appropriate SI units, determine the correct number of significant figures, and calculate percent error.
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever had a measurement really matter — in cooking, sports, building something, or shopping for clothes? What happened when it was off?
lessons.do_now: Three students measure the length of a textbook. Student A gets 27.3 cm, Student B gets 27.34 cm, and Student C gets 27 cm. Which measurement is most precise? Explain your reasoning.
materials: Graduated cylinders — 10 mL and 100 mL (1 of each per group)
Irregular objects for volume measurement (metal bolts, small rocks)

engage.description: Present the 1999 Mars Climate Orbiter disaster: a $125 million spacecraft destroyed because one engineering team used pounds and another used newtons. Display the headline and ask: How could a unit error destroy a spacecraft? Students turn-and-talk, then share out.

explore.description: Station rotation (4 stations, 3 min each): Station 1 — measure length of three objects with a ruler to the correct decimal place. Station 2 — find mass of three objects on a triple-beam balance. Station 3 — measure liquid volume in a graduated cylinder (reading the meniscus). Station 4 — find volume of an irregular solid by water displacement. Students record all measurements with correct units.

explain.description: Direct instruction on significant figures: five rules for counting sig figs, sig figs in calculations (multiplication/division — least sig figs; addition/subtraction — least decimal places). Then introduce percent error formula: % error = |measured - accepted| / accepted x 100%. Work through two examples as a class using the Physics Reference Table.

elaborate.description: Students calculate the density of their irregular solid using mass and volume data from stations. They express the answer with correct significant figures and calculate percent error against the accepted density value provided by the teacher.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) How many significant figures are in 0.00340 m? (2) A student measures the density of aluminum as 2.85 g/cm3. The accepted value is 2.70 g/cm3. Calculate the percent error.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a significant figures decision flowchart (Is it a non-zero digit? -> Always significant. Is it a zero? -> Follow these rules...). Pre-label station recording sheets with units and decimal place guides.
differentiation.on_level: Complete all four measurement stations and sig fig calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Investigate how many sig figs each measuring tool provides and rank them by precision. Calculate the propagation of uncertainty through the density calculation.
differentiation.ell: Provide a bilingual measurement vocabulary card with diagrams showing how to read each instrument. Use color-coded labels on stations (green = length, blue = mass, red = volume).
differentiation.iep: Provide a calculator reference card with the percent error formula pre-loaded as an example. Reduce stations to three. Allow extended time for the exit ticket with a sig fig rules reference card.

lessons.crse_connection: Explore how ancient civilizations developed sophisticated measurement systems — the Egyptian royal cubit (used to build the pyramids with remarkable precision), the Aztec system based on body measurements, and the Chinese chi — and discuss how the need for global scientific collaboration led to the metric system.
lessons.hochman_activity: Appositive sentences: Students write sentences embedding definitions as appositives. Example: 'Percent error, a calculation that compares a measured value to an accepted value, tells us how accurate our measurement is.' Students write two more using 'significant figures' and 'precision.'

vocabulary.definition: The International System of Units — the standard measurement system used in science (meter, kilogram, second, etc.)
The digits in a measurement that are known with certainty plus one estimated digit, indicating the precision of the measurement
How close repeated measurements are to each other; related to the smallest division on the measuring tool
How close a measurement is to the true or accepted value
A calculation that quantifies accuracy: |measured - accepted| / accepted x 100%
The curved upper surface of a liquid in a container, read at the bottom of the curve for most liquids

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: SI Base Units and Common Prefixes (kilo, centi, milli, micro)
Section 2: Rules for Counting Significant Figures
Section 3: Significant Figures in Calculations
Section 4: Accuracy vs. Precision
Section 5: Percent Error Calculations

cer.phenomenon: A pharmaceutical company produces 500 mg aspirin tablets. Quality control requires that each tablet be within 2% of the stated mass. A technician uses a balance precise to the nearest 10 mg and measures five tablets: 500 mg, 510 mg, 490 mg, 500 mg, 510 mg. A second technician uses a balance precise to the nearest 1 mg and measures: 502.3 mg, 498.7 mg, 501.1 mg, 499.8 mg, 500.4 mg.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the measurement data, I claim that Technician ___'s balance is better suited for quality control because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the percent error for each measurement and determine which set of measurements can reliably confirm the tablets are within the 2% tolerance.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because the precision of the instrument determines whether we can ___, and in pharmaceutical quality control, the consequence of insufficient precision is ___.

lessons.title: Graphical Analysis of Physical Relationships
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can construct and interpret graphs of linear, quadratic, and inverse relationships and determine the physical meaning of slope and area under a curve.
lessons.circle_prompt: Where do you see graphs in your daily life — on the news, in sports stats, on social media, in video games? What story was the graph trying to tell?
lessons.do_now: A spring stretches 2 cm for every 1 N of force applied. Sketch what you think the graph of Force vs. Stretch would look like. Label your axes.
materials: Data sets handout (3 relationships: linear, quadratic, inverse)

engage.description: Display three unlabeled graphs: a straight line, a parabola, and a hyperbola. Ask: What real-world situations could each of these represent? Students brainstorm in pairs. Reveal that all three patterns appear frequently in physics and that recognizing them is a key skill for the Regents exam.

explore.description: Groups receive three data sets: (1) Force vs. Acceleration (linear — constant mass), (2) Distance vs. Time for a falling object (quadratic), (3) Pressure vs. Volume of a gas (inverse). Each group graphs one data set on graph paper following the graphing rubric (title, labeled axes with units, appropriate scale, best-fit line/curve). Groups then rotate to view other graphs.

explain.description: Teacher-led discussion: How to identify each relationship from the shape of the graph. For linear graphs: slope = rise/run and has physical meaning (e.g., slope of Force vs. Acceleration = mass). Demonstrate how to calculate slope from two points on the line. Introduce the concept that the area under a velocity-time graph represents displacement. Show how to linearize quadratic and inverse relationships.

elaborate.description: Students receive a velocity-time graph for a car trip. They calculate the slope (acceleration) for two different segments and determine the total displacement by calculating the area under the curve using geometric shapes (rectangles and triangles).

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: Given a position-time graph with two linear segments, students identify which segment shows faster motion, calculate the speed during each segment from the slope, and describe what is happening physically.

differentiation.approaching: Provide pre-scaled and pre-labeled axes for graphing. Include a reference card showing what linear, quadratic, and inverse graphs look like with their equations (y = mx + b, y = kx^2, y = k/x).
differentiation.on_level: Complete graphing activity and slope/area calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Given raw data, determine whether the relationship is linear, quadratic, or inverse by creating a linearized graph (plot y vs. x^2 or y vs. 1/x) and calculating R-squared values.
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual glossary of graph types with labeled examples in English and native language. Use color-coding: blue for linear, red for quadratic, green for inverse throughout all materials.
differentiation.iep: Provide graph templates with pre-drawn axes and scales. Offer a step-by-step slope calculation checklist. Reduce the number of data points to plot from 8 to 5.

lessons.crse_connection: Highlight how Florence Nightingale revolutionized healthcare by using statistical graphs (her polar area diagrams) to convince the British government to improve military hospital conditions — showing how data visualization can be a tool for social justice.
lessons.hochman_activity: Subordinating conjunctions: Students write sentences using 'when,' 'if,' and 'although' with graph analysis vocabulary. Example: 'When the slope of a position-time graph is constant, the object is moving at constant velocity.' Students create two more using 'if' and 'although.'

vocabulary.definition: A relationship between two variables that produces a straight-line graph; described by y = mx + b
A relationship where one variable depends on the square of another; produces a parabolic curve (y = kx^2)
A relationship where one variable increases as the other decreases proportionally; produces a hyperbola (y = k/x)
The ratio of the change in the y-variable to the change in the x-variable (rise over run); represents a rate of change with physical meaning
A straight line drawn through data points that best represents the overall trend, with roughly equal numbers of points above and below

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Rules for Constructing Scientific Graphs (title, axes, units, scale)
Section 2: Linear Relationships and the Meaning of Slope
Section 3: Quadratic and Inverse Relationships — Recognizing the Shape
Section 4: Area Under a Curve and Its Physical Meaning

cer.phenomenon: A student collects data on the stretch of a rubber band as increasing masses are hung from it. For masses 0-300 g, the data forms a straight line. For masses 300-500 g, the rubber band stretches more than expected and the graph curves upward. Above 500 g, the rubber band breaks.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the graphical data, I claim that the rubber band follows a linear relationship only within a certain range because...
cer.evidence_source: Use the shape of the graph in each region (0-300 g, 300-500 g, and the breaking point) to describe how the rubber band's behavior changes.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because the transition from linear to non-linear behavior indicates that ___, which is important in engineering because ___.

lessons.title: Vectors: Representation, Addition, and Components
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can distinguish between scalar and vector quantities, add vectors graphically using the head-to-tail method, and resolve a vector into its x- and y-components using trigonometry.
lessons.circle_prompt: If someone tells you to walk 5 blocks, do you have enough information to find them? What additional information would you need? Why does direction matter?
lessons.do_now: A dog walks 4 m east and then 3 m north. Draw a sketch of the path. How far did the dog walk in total? How far is the dog from where it started? Why are these numbers different?

engage.description: Show a short video of an airplane flying in a crosswind — the plane points one direction but moves in a different direction over the ground. Ask: Why doesn't the plane go where it's pointing? Introduce the idea that motion and forces often combine in ways that require vector thinking.

explore.description: Guided activity: Students use rulers and protractors to perform graphical vector addition. Problem 1: Walk 5.0 cm east, then 3.0 cm north — draw the resultant and measure its length and angle. Problem 2: Two forces act on an object — 8.0 N at 0 degrees and 6.0 N at 90 degrees. Find the resultant graphically. Students discover the head-to-tail method through guided practice.

explain.description: Formalize the concepts: scalar vs. vector quantities (table of examples: distance/displacement, speed/velocity, mass/force). Teach the component method: Ax = A cos(theta), Ay = A sin(theta). Demonstrate finding the resultant from components: R = sqrt(Rx^2 + Ry^2) and theta = tan^-1(Ry/Rx). Work through one full example with a 50 N force at 37 degrees above horizontal.

elaborate.description: Application problem: A river current flows east at 3.0 m/s. A swimmer heads north at 4.0 m/s relative to the water. Students find the swimmer's resultant velocity (magnitude and direction) using both graphical and component methods and compare their answers.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A force of 100 N acts at 30 degrees above the horizontal. Calculate the horizontal and vertical components. Then: Is temperature a scalar or vector? Explain.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a step-by-step vector addition checklist with diagrams. Include a pre-drawn coordinate grid for graphical addition. Supply a SOH-CAH-TOA reference triangle on every worksheet.
differentiation.on_level: Complete graphical and component vector addition problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Solve a three-vector addition problem using the component method (e.g., three forces at different angles acting on a ring). Calculate equilibrant force.
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual scalar vs. vector comparison chart with icons (arrow for vector, number for scalar). Use color-coding for x-components (red) and y-components (blue) throughout. Sentence frames for explaining direction.
differentiation.iep: Provide a calculator tutorial card showing how to use sin, cos, and tan functions. Break the component method into a numbered checklist. Allow use of the graphical method for all problems if the component method is challenging.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how navigation has been essential across cultures — Polynesian wayfinders used star positions and ocean currents (vector reasoning) to navigate thousands of miles across the Pacific without instruments, demonstrating sophisticated understanding of combining directional quantities.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'vector' and 'scalar': Speed is a scalar quantity because___. Velocity and speed both describe how fast something moves, but___. The wind blows north while the boat heads east, so the resultant velocity___.

vocabulary.definition: A quantity that has only magnitude (size), such as mass, speed, distance, time, and energy
A quantity that has both magnitude and direction, such as displacement, velocity, acceleration, and force
The single vector that has the same effect as two or more vectors combined; found by vector addition
The projection of a vector along an axis; any vector can be broken into perpendicular x- and y-components
A single vector that, when added to a system of vectors, produces a net result of zero — equal in magnitude but opposite in direction to the resultant
A graphical technique for adding vectors by placing the tail of each successive vector at the head of the previous one; the resultant goes from the first tail to the last head

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Scalars vs. Vectors — What's the Difference?
Section 2: Representing Vectors — Arrows, Angles, and Notation
Section 3: Graphical Vector Addition (Head-to-Tail Method)
Section 4: Vector Components Using Trigonometry (SOH-CAH-TOA)
Section 5: Finding the Resultant from Components

cer.phenomenon: A pilot needs to fly from New York to Boston, a distance of 300 km due northeast (45 degrees). However, a wind blows from the west at 80 km/h. The plane's airspeed is 250 km/h. The pilot points the plane directly toward Boston but lands east of the destination.
cer.claim_starter: Based on vector analysis, I claim that the pilot missed Boston because...
cer.evidence_source: Draw a vector diagram showing the plane's velocity vector and the wind velocity vector. Use the head-to-tail method to find the resultant velocity and its direction.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because the resultant of the plane's velocity and the wind velocity produces a ground track that ___, which means the pilot should have aimed ___ to compensate.

units.title: Kinematics — 1D & 2D Motion
units.anchoring_phenomenon: During the 2009 World Championships, Usain Bolt ran the 100 m dash in 9.58 seconds. His average speed was 10.44 m/s, but at his fastest he reached 12.27 m/s. How can his top speed be so different from his average speed, and what does his motion look like at each moment of the race?
essential_questions: How do we describe and predict the motion of objects in one and two dimensions?
What does the shape of a motion graph tell us about how an object moves?
How does gravity shape the path of a projectile?
units.crse_theme: Students analyze the physics of motion in sports and cultural contexts — sprinting biomechanics across different athletic traditions, the physics of traditional games like cricket bowling and capoeira movements, and how motion analysis technology is used to reduce injuries in athletes from underserved communities.

summative: Investigation: Acceleration Due to Gravity Lab

investigations: Investigation 2: Determining the Acceleration Due to Gravity Using a Free-Falling Object

lessons.title: Distance, Displacement, Speed, and Velocity
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can distinguish between distance and displacement and between speed and velocity, and calculate each from given information.
lessons.circle_prompt: What's the fastest you've ever traveled — in a car, train, plane, roller coaster, or on foot? How did it feel? What did you notice about your body?
lessons.do_now: You walk from your home to school: 3 blocks east, then 4 blocks north. What is the total distance you walked? What is your displacement? Draw a diagram to help.
materials: Meter sticks or measuring tapes (1 per group)
Whiteboard markers and mini-whiteboards (1 per student)

engage.description: A student volunteer walks a winding path around the classroom (marked with tape on the floor) and returns to their starting point. The class measures the path length (~15 m). Ask: How far did they travel? How far are they from where they started? Why is the second answer zero? This introduces the distance vs. displacement distinction viscerally.

explore.description: In pairs, students walk two different paths between the same two points in the hallway, timing each walk. Path A: straight line. Path B: an L-shaped detour. They calculate average speed (distance/time) and average velocity (displacement/time) for each path. Students record data and compare results.

explain.description: Formalize definitions: distance (scalar, total path length) vs. displacement (vector, straight-line from start to finish with direction). Speed (scalar, distance/time) vs. velocity (vector, displacement/time). Emphasize units: m/s. Work through two practice problems: (1) A jogger runs around a 400 m track in 80 s — find average speed and average velocity. (2) A car drives 100 km north in 1 hour, then 100 km south in 1 hour.

elaborate.description: Map activity: Using a simplified grid map of the school neighborhood, students calculate the distance and displacement for a route from the school to a nearby landmark. They express displacement with magnitude and compass direction.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A delivery drone flies 400 m north, then 300 m east. Calculate: (a) total distance traveled, (b) magnitude of displacement, (c) average speed if the trip takes 70 seconds, (d) magnitude of average velocity.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a comparison chart template (Distance vs. Displacement, Speed vs. Velocity) with column headers pre-filled. Include a worked example on the back of the worksheet.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the hallway walking activity and practice problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate the direction of displacement using trigonometry and express average velocity as a vector with magnitude and angle. Analyze a multi-leg trip with three segments.
differentiation.ell: Use physical demonstrations (walking) to reinforce concepts before abstract calculation. Provide a bilingual Distance/Displacement visual reference card. Allow pointing to diagrams when explaining reasoning.
differentiation.iep: Provide a formula card with d = v x t clearly displayed. Use the hallway activity as the primary assessment rather than the written exit ticket. Break the exit ticket into single-step parts with space for diagrams.

lessons.crse_connection: Analyze Usain Bolt's 100 m world record sprint using real split-time data, connecting to the physics of sprinting biomechanics. Discuss how Jamaican sprint training programs have produced world-class athletes and the cultural significance of track and field in Caribbean communities.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'displacement': A runner who completes a lap around a track has zero displacement because___. Distance and displacement may have the same magnitude, but___. The drone flew north and then east, so its displacement was___.

vocabulary.definition: The total length of the path traveled by an object; a scalar quantity measured in meters
The straight-line distance and direction from an object's initial position to its final position; a vector quantity
The rate at which an object covers distance; speed = distance / time; a scalar quantity in m/s
The rate at which an object changes its position; velocity = displacement / time; a vector quantity in m/s with direction
Total distance divided by total time for an entire trip
Total displacement divided by total time; can be zero even when average speed is not

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Distance vs. Displacement — Scalar and Vector
Section 2: Speed vs. Velocity — Scalar and Vector
Section 3: Calculating Average Speed and Average Velocity
Section 4: When Displacement Equals Zero but Distance Does Not

cer.phenomenon: A New York City taxi picks up a passenger at 42nd Street and 8th Avenue. It drives 5 blocks east to 42nd and 3rd Avenue, then 3 blocks north to 45th and 3rd Avenue, then 5 blocks west to 45th and 8th Avenue. The total trip takes 8 minutes. The fare is based on distance traveled.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the taxi's route, I claim that the fare (based on distance) is significantly more than what the passenger would pay if fares were based on displacement because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the total distance driven and the magnitude of displacement from pickup to drop-off. Assume each block is approximately 80 m (east-west) or 80 m (north-south).
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because the winding route adds ___ to the total path length, while the displacement is only ___, showing that distance and displacement can differ significantly when ___.

lessons.title: Position-Time Graphs and Instantaneous Velocity
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can interpret position-time graphs to describe an object's motion and calculate instantaneous and average velocity from the graph.
lessons.circle_prompt: If you could see a replay of your entire day as a dot moving on a map, when would the dot be moving fastest? When would it be still? What story would the path tell?
lessons.do_now: Sketch a position-time graph for the following: A student walks forward at a steady pace for 5 seconds, stops for 3 seconds, then walks backward slowly for 4 seconds. Label your axes.
materials: Motion detector or sonic ranger (1 per group, or teacher demo)
Pre-printed position-time graph sets (4 graphs per sheet)

engage.description: Teacher demonstration: Connect a motion detector to a display. Walk toward and away from the sensor at different speeds while the class watches the real-time position-time graph form. Ask students to predict what the graph will look like before each motion, then compare. Students see that constant velocity = straight line, faster = steeper, stopped = horizontal.

explore.description: Challenge activity: Display a target position-time graph on the screen. Students take turns walking in front of the motion detector trying to match the graph with their body motion. Start with simple graphs (constant velocity) and progress to complex ones (changing direction, speeding up). If motion detectors are unavailable, students work in pairs: one describes a motion verbally, the other draws the graph, then compare.

explain.description: Formalize graph interpretation: slope of position-time graph = velocity. Positive slope = forward motion, negative slope = backward motion, zero slope = at rest, steeper slope = faster. Demonstrate how to calculate average velocity between two points (slope of secant line) and introduce instantaneous velocity as the slope at a single point (slope of tangent line). Work through two examples from printed graphs.

elaborate.description: Students receive a complex position-time graph showing a car's journey through a city. They answer: (1) During which time interval was the car moving fastest? (2) When was the car stopped? (3) When did the car return toward its starting point? (4) Calculate the average velocity for the entire trip.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: Given a position-time graph with two segments (one steep positive slope, one gentle negative slope), calculate the velocity during each segment and write a sentence describing the motion.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a position-time graph interpretation key with example graphs paired with motion descriptions. Include a slope calculation template (pick two points, subtract, divide).
differentiation.on_level: Complete motion detector matching activity and graph interpretation problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Given a position-time curve (not a straight line), estimate instantaneous velocity at multiple points by drawing tangent lines. Create a velocity-time graph from the position-time data.
differentiation.ell: Use physical motion demonstrations alongside every graph. Provide a word bank of motion descriptions (moving forward, moving backward, at rest, speeding up, slowing down) in English and native language. Pair verbal descriptions with graph annotations.
differentiation.iep: Color-code graph segments (green = moving forward, red = moving backward, yellow = stopped). Provide a simplified graph with only two segments for analysis. Allow verbal description of motion instead of written sentences.

lessons.crse_connection: Explore how GPS technology — originally developed for military use — now powers apps like Google Maps and Waze that millions of people in urban communities rely on daily. Discuss how the physics of position-time tracking has made navigation accessible to everyone, regardless of their familiarity with an area.
lessons.hochman_activity: Subordinating conjunctions: Students write three sentences about position-time graphs using 'while,' 'because,' and 'although.' Example: 'While the slope of the graph is positive, the object moves in the positive direction.'

vocabulary.definition: A graph that shows an object's position on the y-axis and time on the x-axis; its slope represents velocity
The velocity of an object at a specific moment in time; found from the slope of the tangent line on a position-time graph
The total displacement divided by the total time interval; found from the slope of a secant line connecting two points on a position-time graph
A line that touches a curve at exactly one point and represents the slope (instantaneous rate of change) at that point
A line connecting two points on a curve; its slope represents the average rate of change between those points

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Reading a Position-Time Graph — What Each Feature Means
Section 2: Slope = Velocity — Connecting the Graph to the Motion
Section 3: Average Velocity from a Position-Time Graph
Section 4: Instantaneous Velocity and the Tangent Line

cer.phenomenon: Two runners compete in a 200 m race. Runner A's position-time graph is a straight line from (0,0) to (25 s, 200 m). Runner B's graph is a curve that starts with a gentle slope and gets steeper, also reaching (25 s, 200 m). Both runners finish at the same time.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the position-time graphs, I claim that Runner B has a higher instantaneous velocity at the finish line than Runner A because...
cer.evidence_source: Compare the slopes of each runner's graph at the finish line (t = 25 s). Consider that Runner A's slope is constant while Runner B's slope is increasing.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because the slope of a position-time graph represents ___, and since Runner B's curve steepens over time, at the finish line the tangent line slope must be ___ than Runner A's constant slope.

lessons.title: Acceleration and Velocity-Time Graphs
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define acceleration as the rate of change of velocity, calculate acceleration from data or velocity-time graphs, and determine displacement from the area under a velocity-time graph.
lessons.circle_prompt: Share a time when you accelerated — speeding up, slowing down, or changing direction. What did it feel like in your body? Where did you feel it?
lessons.do_now: A car goes from 0 to 60 mph in 6 seconds. A bicycle goes from 0 to 15 mph in 6 seconds. Both took the same time. Which one accelerated more? How do you know?
materials: Colored pencils for shading area under curves

engage.description: Show a slow-motion video of a cheetah accelerating from rest to chase prey, with a speedometer overlay. Ask: The cheetah reaches 70 mph in 3 seconds. What is its acceleration in m/s^2? (Convert first.) Then show a Tesla Model S doing 0-60 mph in 2.3 seconds. Which accelerates more? Students predict, then calculate.

explore.description: Students receive six velocity-time graphs showing different motions: constant velocity, constant positive acceleration, constant negative acceleration (deceleration), an object at rest, an object that speeds up then slows down, and an object that changes direction. For each graph, students describe the motion in words, calculate the acceleration (slope), and shade the area under the curve to find displacement.

explain.description: Define acceleration: a = (vf - vi) / t, with units m/s^2. Emphasize that acceleration is a vector — negative acceleration means acceleration in the negative direction, not necessarily slowing down. Walk through velocity-time graph interpretation: slope = acceleration, area under curve = displacement. Demonstrate calculating area using rectangles and triangles for a graph with two segments.

elaborate.description: Real-world application: Students analyze a velocity-time graph of Usain Bolt's 100 m world record sprint (using published split data converted to velocity). They identify the phase of greatest acceleration (first 4 seconds), calculate his average acceleration during that phase, and determine the total displacement by estimating area under the curve.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A velocity-time graph shows an object starting at 10 m/s, accelerating uniformly to 30 m/s over 5 seconds. (a) What is the acceleration? (b) What is the displacement during this time? (c) Is the object speeding up or slowing down?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a velocity-time graph interpretation guide with annotated examples. Include a formula card: a = (vf - vi)/t and area = base x height for rectangles, area = 1/2 x base x height for triangles. Pre-shade one graph as a model.
differentiation.on_level: Complete all six velocity-time graph analyses and the Usain Bolt application as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Given a position-time graph (curved), sketch the corresponding velocity-time graph and acceleration-time graph. Analyze whether the object's speed is increasing, decreasing, or constant at various points.
differentiation.ell: Create a motion description word bank in English and native language (speeding up, slowing down, constant speed, at rest, changing direction). Pair each velocity-time graph with a physical motion description and a simple stick-figure animation.
differentiation.iep: Provide graphs with grid lines to facilitate easier area calculations. Reduce the number of graphs to analyze from six to four. Include a worked example on the front of the handout. Allow use of calculator for all computations.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how acceleration data from smartphones is being used by researchers at Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs) to study earthquake preparedness in underserved communities, showing how physics concepts have direct applications in protecting vulnerable populations.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'acceleration': A car has a negative acceleration because___. A ball thrown upward has a negative acceleration, but its velocity is initially positive, so___. The area under a velocity-time graph represents displacement, so to find how far an object traveled, you must___.

vocabulary.definition: The rate of change of velocity with respect to time; a = (vf - vi) / t; a vector quantity measured in m/s^2
Acceleration that does not change over time, producing a straight line on a velocity-time graph
A decrease in speed; occurs when acceleration is in the opposite direction of velocity (informal term — in physics, it is simply acceleration in the opposite direction)
A graph with velocity on the y-axis and time on the x-axis; slope = acceleration, area under curve = displacement
Motion at constant velocity (zero acceleration), represented by a horizontal line on a velocity-time graph

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Defining Acceleration — Rate of Change of Velocity
Section 2: Calculating Acceleration from Data
Section 3: Reading Velocity-Time Graphs — Slope and Area
Section 4: Positive, Negative, and Zero Acceleration
Section 5: Connecting Position-Time and Velocity-Time Graphs

cer.phenomenon: A roller coaster at Six Flags starts from rest at the top of a 60 m drop. Sensors record the following velocity data: t=0 s, v=0 m/s; t=1 s, v=9.8 m/s; t=2 s, v=19.6 m/s; t=3 s, v=25.0 m/s; t=4 s, v=27.0 m/s. The coaster reaches the bottom of the hill at t=4 s.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the velocity data, I claim that the roller coaster's acceleration is not constant throughout the drop because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the acceleration during each one-second interval and compare the values. Create a velocity-time graph and examine whether the data forms a straight line.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because constant acceleration would produce ___ on a velocity-time graph, but the data shows ___, which suggests that ___ (such as air resistance) affects the acceleration as speed increases.

lessons.title: Kinematic Equations for Constant Acceleration
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can select and apply the appropriate kinematic equation to solve problems involving constant acceleration in one dimension.
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever had to make a quick calculation in real life — figuring out if you could make it across the street before a car arrived, or whether you had enough time to catch a bus? How did you estimate?
lessons.do_now: A car accelerates from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 4 seconds. Without using any formulas, estimate how far the car traveled. Explain your reasoning. (Hint: think about the average velocity.)

engage.description: Present a real scenario: A driver sees a red light 80 m ahead while traveling at 25 m/s. If the car decelerates at -3.0 m/s^2, will it stop in time? Tell students that by the end of class, they will be able to answer this question precisely. Ask for predictions first — thumbs up (stops in time) or thumbs down.

explore.description: Introduce the four kinematic equations from the Physics Reference Table: (1) vf = vi + at, (2) d = vit + 1/2at^2, (3) vf^2 = vi^2 + 2ad, (4) d = (vi + vf)/2 x t. Students work in pairs to create a chart: for each equation, list the five variables (vi, vf, a, d, t) and circle which one is MISSING. This becomes their equation selection strategy: identify the variable you don't know and don't need, then pick the equation that doesn't contain it.

explain.description: Model the problem-solving strategy: (1) List knowns and unknowns. (2) Identify which variable is not given and not asked for. (3) Select the equation missing that variable. (4) Substitute and solve with units. (5) Check: Does the answer make sense? Work through two examples: the red-light problem from Engage and a rocket launching vertically with constant acceleration.

elaborate.description: Students work through tiered problems independently: Level 1 — direct plug-in (given vi, a, t, find d). Level 2 — requires solving for an intermediate variable first. Level 3 — multi-step context problems (a train accelerating out of a station, a skateboarder going down a hill). Students self-select starting level.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A ball rolls down a ramp starting from rest and accelerates at 2.0 m/s^2. How far does it travel in 3.0 seconds? What is its final velocity?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a kinematic equation selection flowchart: 'What variable is missing? -> Use this equation.' Include a worked example for each equation type. Pre-organize problems as Step 1: List knowns, Step 2: Choose equation, Step 3: Substitute, Step 4: Solve.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the equation selection chart and tiered problem set, working through at least Levels 1 and 2.
differentiation.advanced: Solve multi-object problems (two cars starting at different times, one chasing the other) and determine when/where they meet. Derive kinematic equations from the definitions of acceleration and the area under a v-t graph.
differentiation.ell: Provide a bilingual physics problem glossary (starts from rest = vi = 0, comes to a stop = vf = 0, uniform acceleration = a is constant). Use visual problem diagrams with labeled arrows for each practice problem.
differentiation.iep: Provide a laminated formula card that stays on the desk. Break each problem into numbered micro-steps with blanks to fill in. Reduce problem set to 6 problems (2 per level). Allow extended time.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how kinematic equations are essential in automotive safety testing — connecting to Ralph Nader's 'Unsafe at Any Speed' and how crash testing disproportionately failed to account for diverse body types until recent advocacy led to more inclusive testing standards.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using kinematic vocabulary: An object starts from rest, so its initial velocity equals___. The kinematic equations only work for constant acceleration, but many real-world situations involve changing acceleration, so___. A car decelerates at -3 m/s^2 because___.

vocabulary.definition: A set of four equations that relate displacement, initial velocity, final velocity, acceleration, and time for objects moving with constant acceleration
The velocity of an object at the beginning of a time interval; 'starts from rest' means vi = 0
The velocity of an object at the end of a time interval; 'comes to a stop' means vf = 0
Acceleration that remains the same throughout the motion, required for the kinematic equations to apply
The change in position of an object; in kinematic equations, the straight-line distance with direction traveled during the time interval

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: The Four Kinematic Equations — What Each Solves
Section 2: Strategy for Choosing the Right Equation
Section 3: Problem-Solving Steps with Worked Examples
Section 4: Special Cases — Starting from Rest, Coming to a Stop

cer.phenomenon: A highway safety study compares stopping distances for cars traveling at different speeds on dry pavement. At 15 m/s (about 34 mph), the stopping distance is 18.75 m. At 30 m/s (about 67 mph), the stopping distance is 75 m. The deceleration due to braking is the same in both cases (-6.0 m/s^2).
cer.claim_starter: Based on the data and kinematic analysis, I claim that doubling the speed more than doubles the stopping distance because...
cer.evidence_source: Use the kinematic equation vf^2 = vi^2 + 2ad to calculate the stopping distance for each initial speed. Compare the ratio of stopping distances to the ratio of speeds.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because stopping distance depends on the ___ of initial velocity (since vf^2 = vi^2 + 2ad and vf = 0 gives d = vi^2 / 2a), so doubling vi ___ the stopping distance. This has implications for speed limits because ___.

lessons.title: Free Fall and the Acceleration Due to Gravity
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can apply kinematic equations to objects in free fall, using g = 9.81 m/s^2 as the acceleration, and predict the motion of objects dropped or thrown vertically.
lessons.circle_prompt: If you dropped a bowling ball and a feather from the same height, which would hit the ground first? What if there were no air? Have you ever seen a demonstration of this?
lessons.do_now: A ball is dropped from a 45 m tall building. Using g = 9.81 m/s^2, estimate how long it takes to hit the ground. (Hint: use d = 1/2 gt^2 and solve for t.)
materials: Tennis balls and baseballs (1 per group)
Meter sticks (2 per group, taped together for 2 m drops)
Video recording devices (student phones for slow-motion)

engage.description: Show the famous Apollo 15 hammer-feather drop on the Moon by astronaut David Scott. Both hit the lunar surface at the same time. Ask: Why don't we see this on Earth? What would change if we could remove air? Establish that in free fall (no air resistance), all objects accelerate at the same rate regardless of mass.

explore.description: Lab mini-investigation: Students drop a tennis ball from a measured height (2.0 m) and use slow-motion video to measure the fall time. They calculate g from d = 1/2gt^2. Then they drop a baseball from the same height and compare the fall time. Groups calculate percent error against the accepted value of 9.81 m/s^2 and discuss sources of error (reaction time, air resistance).

explain.description: Formalize free fall: define as motion under gravity alone (no air resistance). Sign convention: if down is positive, a = +9.81 m/s^2; if up is positive, a = -9.81 m/s^2. Work through three problem types: (1) Object dropped from rest — find time and final velocity. (2) Object thrown straight down with initial velocity. (3) Object thrown straight up — find max height, total time in air, and velocity when it returns to launch height.

elaborate.description: Real-world application: The world record for the highest skydive is held by Alan Eustace, who jumped from 41,425 m. If he were in true free fall (no air resistance) from that height, how fast would he be going when he reached the ground? Students calculate and convert to mph, then discuss why the actual speed was much lower (air resistance, terminal velocity preview).

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A ball is thrown straight up with an initial velocity of 19.6 m/s. (a) How high does it go? (b) How long until it reaches the highest point? (c) What is the velocity at the highest point?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a free-fall problem template: 'Object dropped' means vi = 0 and a = 9.81 m/s^2 down. 'Object thrown up' means a = -9.81 m/s^2 and vf = 0 at the top. Include a sign convention diagram on every worksheet.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the drop investigation and all three problem types as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Analyze the full up-and-down motion of an object thrown upward: create position-time, velocity-time, and acceleration-time graphs for the entire trip. Calculate the velocity at any height during both the upward and downward trip.
differentiation.ell: Use slow-motion video playback to connect physical observations with equations. Provide visual sign convention chart in English and native language. Use arrows consistently (up arrow = positive) on all diagrams.
differentiation.iep: Provide a free-fall equation reference card with the two most common setups pre-organized (dropped from rest, thrown upward). Break the ball-thrown-up problem into three separate sub-problems. Allow calculator use throughout.

lessons.crse_connection: Highlight the contributions of Galileo Galilei, who challenged the Aristotelian belief that heavier objects fall faster. Connect to how questioning established authority in science parallels social justice movements that challenge entrenched systems — both require evidence, courage, and persistence.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'free fall': A feather falls slower than a rock on Earth because___. In a vacuum, a feather and a rock would fall at the same rate, but on Earth___. At the highest point of its path, a ball thrown upward has zero velocity, so___.

vocabulary.definition: The motion of an object under the influence of gravity alone, with no air resistance; all objects in free fall accelerate at the same rate
The acceleration experienced by objects in free fall near Earth's surface; g = 9.81 m/s^2 directed downward
The constant velocity reached when air resistance equals the gravitational force on a falling object, resulting in zero net force and zero acceleration
The sensation experienced during free fall when there is no normal force acting on a person; the person and their surroundings accelerate at the same rate
The choice of which direction is positive and which is negative; must be consistent throughout a problem

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: What Is Free Fall? — Gravity as the Only Force
Section 2: The Value of g and Sign Conventions
Section 3: Objects Dropped from Rest
Section 4: Objects Thrown Vertically Upward
Section 5: Symmetry of Free-Fall Motion

cer.phenomenon: During the Red Bull Stratos project, Felix Baumgartner jumped from a capsule at 39,045 m altitude. He was in free fall for 4 minutes and 19 seconds before deploying his parachute at 1,524 m altitude. He reached a maximum speed of 373 m/s (Mach 1.25). If he had been in true free fall (no air resistance) for the same duration (259 seconds), he would have reached a speed of 2,541 m/s.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the data, I claim that air resistance significantly affected Baumgartner's fall because...
cer.evidence_source: Compare the predicted free-fall velocity (using vf = vi + gt with g = 9.81 m/s^2) with his actual maximum velocity of 373 m/s.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because the kinematic prediction assumes ___, but in reality ___ acts as an opposing force that increases with speed, which is why his maximum velocity was only ___% of the predicted value.

lessons.title: Projectile Motion — Horizontally Launched
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can analyze the motion of a horizontally launched projectile by independently solving the horizontal and vertical components of motion.
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever thrown something off a ledge or a balcony — a paper airplane, a ball, a frisbee? Did it go straight down or curve forward? What shape did the path make?
lessons.do_now: A marble rolls off a table at 2.0 m/s. The table is 1.0 m high. Sketch the path you think the marble takes after leaving the table. Does the horizontal speed change? Does the vertical speed change?
materials: Marbles and ramps (for table-edge launch demonstrations)
Carbon paper and white paper (to mark landing spot)

engage.description: Teacher demonstration: Simultaneously drop a marble from the edge of the table and launch another marble horizontally from the same height at the same moment. Students listen for two sounds when the marbles hit the floor. Key question: Do both marbles hit the ground at the same time? (Yes!) Why? This reveals that horizontal and vertical motions are independent.

explore.description: Lab activity: Students launch a marble off the edge of a table at a known horizontal speed (controlled by ramp height). They measure the table height, predict the landing distance using projectile equations, then measure the actual landing spot (marked with carbon paper). Groups compare predictions to results and calculate percent error.

explain.description: Teach the independence of horizontal and vertical motion: Horizontal — no acceleration, vx is constant, dx = vx*t. Vertical — acceleration due to gravity, initial vertical velocity = 0 for horizontal launch, dy = 1/2*g*t^2. The key link: TIME is the same for both. Problem-solving strategy: Use the vertical equations to find time, then use time in horizontal equations to find range. Work through a full example: a stunt car drives off a 20 m cliff at 15 m/s.

elaborate.description: Students solve: A rescue helicopter flies horizontally at 40 m/s at an altitude of 200 m and must drop a supply package to people on the ground. How far before the target (horizontal distance) should the pilot release the package? Students also sketch the path of the package as seen from the ground.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A ball is kicked horizontally off a 45 m tall cliff with a speed of 8.0 m/s. (a) How long does it take to hit the ground? (b) How far from the base of the cliff does it land? (c) What is the vertical velocity just before impact?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a two-column problem-solving template: left column for horizontal calculations, right column for vertical calculations, with a bridge between them labeled 'TIME is the same.' Include the equations pre-written in each column.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the marble prediction lab and practice problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate the velocity vector (magnitude and direction) of the projectile at impact using the Pythagorean theorem and inverse tangent. Predict where a projectile would land on a sloped surface.
differentiation.ell: Use animations showing horizontal and vertical components separately before combining them. Provide a visual T-chart template with icons (horizontal arrow, vertical arrow) and equations labeled in both English and native language.
differentiation.iep: Break projectile problems into explicit steps: Step 1 — Find time from vertical info. Step 2 — Use time in horizontal equation. Provide a worked example permanently visible on the board. Reduce practice problems to three.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how understanding projectile motion was critical in the engineering of aqueducts across civilizations — Roman, Incan, and Khmer — and how water distribution systems designed centuries ago in diverse cultures used the physics of projectile motion to bring water to communities.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'projectile motion': The horizontal velocity of a projectile remains constant because___. A marble dropped and a marble launched horizontally from the same height hit the ground at the same time, but___. The vertical velocity increases during projectile motion, so the path curves___.

vocabulary.definition: Any object launched into the air that moves under the influence of gravity alone (ignoring air resistance)
The curved path followed by a projectile; a parabola for objects in uniform gravitational fields
The part of a projectile's motion parallel to the ground; constant velocity because there is no horizontal acceleration (ignoring air resistance)
The part of a projectile's motion perpendicular to the ground; accelerated by gravity at 9.81 m/s^2 downward
The horizontal distance traveled by a projectile from launch to landing
The principle that horizontal and vertical components of projectile motion do not affect each other

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: What Makes an Object a Projectile?
Section 2: Independence of Horizontal and Vertical Motion
Section 3: Equations for Horizontally Launched Projectiles
Section 4: Problem-Solving Strategy — The Two-Column Method
Section 5: The Velocity Vector at Any Point During Flight

cer.phenomenon: During a basketball game, a player standing at the free throw line (4.6 m from the basket) shoots the ball horizontally from a height of 2.5 m. The basket rim is 3.05 m above the floor. The ball leaves the player's hands at a horizontal speed of 5.0 m/s.
cer.claim_starter: Based on projectile motion analysis, I claim that a ball launched horizontally from the free throw line will not go into the basket because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the time for the ball to travel 4.6 m horizontally and determine how far the ball falls vertically in that time. Compare the final height with the rim height of 3.05 m.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because a horizontally launched projectile always ___ due to gravity, so after traveling 4.6 m horizontally the ball would be at a height of ___, which is ___ the rim. This is why basketball players always launch the ball at an ___ above horizontal.

lessons.title: Projectile Motion — Angled Launch Introduction
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can resolve the initial velocity of an angled projectile into horizontal and vertical components and use them to calculate maximum height, total time, and range.
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about throwing a ball as far as you can. What angle would you throw it at? Why not straight up? Why not at a very low angle? What's the sweet spot?
lessons.do_now: A soccer ball is kicked at 20 m/s at an angle of 30 degrees above the ground. Calculate the horizontal component (vx = v cos 30) and the vertical component (vy = v sin 30) of the initial velocity.
materials: Scientific calculators with trig functions (1 per student)
Projectile motion simulation (PhET or similar) on devices

engage.description: Show a slow-motion video of a soccer goalkeeper's goal kick. The ball travels in a symmetric arc. Ask: What determines how far the ball goes — the speed, the angle, or both? Use a PhET projectile simulation to launch the same speed at 30, 45, 60, and 75 degrees. Students observe which angle produces the maximum range (45 degrees) and discuss why.

explore.description: Using the PhET simulation, students launch projectiles at 45 degrees with different speeds and record the range, max height, and total time. Then they launch at the same speed but different angles (15, 30, 45, 60, 75 degrees). They discover that complementary angles (30 and 60, 15 and 75) give the same range and that 45 degrees maximizes range.

explain.description: Teach the full solution method for angled launches: Step 1 — Resolve vi into components: vx = vi cos(theta), vy = vi sin(theta). Step 2 — Use vy and vertical equations to find time to max height (vy_final = 0) and total time (symmetry: total time = 2 x time to top). Step 3 — Use vx and total time to find range. Step 4 — Use vy to find max height. Work through a complete example: a football punted at 22 m/s at 55 degrees.

elaborate.description: Real-world problem: A long jumper leaves the ground at 9.0 m/s at an angle of 22 degrees above horizontal. Calculate the range of the jump. Then discuss: Why don't long jumpers launch at 45 degrees? (Because they can't maintain the same speed at a steeper launch angle — biomechanics limit the angle.)

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A cannonball is fired at 50 m/s at 37 degrees above horizontal. (a) Find vx and vy. (b) How long until it reaches maximum height? (c) What is the maximum height?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a step-by-step angled projectile template with blanks: 'Step 1: vx = ___ x cos(___) = ___. Step 2: vy = ___ x sin(___) = ___.' Include a calculator keystroke guide for trig functions.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the simulation exploration and angled launch problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Solve for the launch angle needed to hit a target at a known distance and height (requires quadratic formula). Analyze why there are typically two angles that can hit the same target on level ground.
differentiation.ell: Use the PhET simulation as a primary learning tool — visual trajectory allows understanding before mathematical formalism. Provide a labeled diagram of the angled launch with all components and variables annotated in English and native language.
differentiation.iep: Allow use of the simulation to check answers after calculating. Provide the trig values for common angles (30, 37, 45, 53, 60 degrees) on a reference card. Reduce the number of practice problems.

lessons.crse_connection: Explore how the physics of projectile motion is central to cricket bowling — a sport with deep cultural significance in South Asian, Caribbean, and British communities. Analyze how bowlers use launch angle and speed to create different types of deliveries.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'launch angle': A projectile launched at 45 degrees achieves maximum range because___. The horizontal and vertical components of velocity change independently, but the launch angle determines the ratio of initial components, so___. Two complementary angles (like 30 and 60 degrees) produce the same range because___.

vocabulary.definition: The angle above the horizontal at which a projectile is launched; determines the ratio of horizontal to vertical velocity components
The highest point reached by a projectile; occurs when the vertical velocity momentarily equals zero
The total horizontal distance traveled by a projectile; maximized at a 45-degree launch angle (on level ground, ignoring air resistance)
The total time a projectile is in the air from launch to landing
Two angles that sum to 90 degrees (e.g., 30 and 60); projectiles launched at complementary angles with the same speed have the same range on level ground

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Resolving Initial Velocity into Components
Section 2: Finding Time of Flight from Vertical Motion
Section 3: Calculating Maximum Height
Section 4: Calculating Range
Section 5: The Special Case of 45 Degrees and Complementary Angles

cer.phenomenon: In the 2024 Olympics shot put event, the winning throw traveled 23.20 m. The shot putter released the 7.26 kg shot from a height of 2.1 m above the ground at approximately 14.5 m/s. Shot putters typically release between 37 and 42 degrees rather than the 45 degrees that maximizes range on level ground.
cer.claim_starter: Based on projectile motion analysis, I claim that the optimal release angle for shot put is less than 45 degrees because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the range for a release at 14.5 m/s from 2.1 m height at both 42 and 45 degrees. Note that the ball is released above ground level, not from the ground.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because when a projectile is launched from above the landing surface, the trajectory is asymmetric — the projectile travels ___ on the way down than on the way up. This shifts the optimal angle ___ than 45 degrees because the additional vertical height from a higher angle provides less benefit than the additional horizontal speed from a ___.

lessons.title: Relative Motion
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can describe the velocity of an object relative to different frames of reference and solve relative motion problems in one and two dimensions.
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever been on a train and felt like the train next to you was moving when it was really your train that started moving? Why does that trick your brain?
lessons.do_now: You are on a bus traveling east at 20 m/s. You walk toward the front of the bus at 1.5 m/s. How fast are you moving relative to the ground? What if you walked toward the back?
materials: Toy cars or rolling carts (2 per group)

engage.description: Show a video of a person walking on a moving walkway at an airport. Ask: If the walkway moves at 1.5 m/s and the person walks at 1.0 m/s in the same direction, how fast do they move relative to the floor? What if they walk against the walkway? What if they walk perpendicular (stepping off the side)? Students predict and discuss.

explore.description: Hands-on activity: Student A slowly pushes a toy car east across a desk while Student B rolls a small ball north across the top of the moving car. The class observes the path of the ball relative to the car (straight north) and relative to the desk (diagonal — northeast). Students sketch both paths and discuss why they look different from different frames of reference.

explain.description: Introduce the relative velocity equation: v_AC = v_AB + v_BC (velocity of A relative to C = velocity of A relative to B + velocity of B relative to C). Emphasize subscript reading: 'A relative to B.' Work through 1D examples (same direction, opposite direction) and one 2D example (boat crossing a river with a current). Show how the vector addition from Unit 1 directly applies.

elaborate.description: River-crossing problem: A boat can travel at 5.0 m/s in still water. The river current flows east at 3.0 m/s. If the boat aims straight north, what is its velocity relative to the shore (magnitude and direction)? How far downstream does it end up after crossing a 100 m wide river? Students solve and then determine what angle the boat should aim upstream to travel straight across.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: Two cars approach an intersection. Car A travels east at 25 m/s. Car B travels north at 15 m/s. What is the velocity of Car A relative to Car B? (Include magnitude and direction.)

differentiation.approaching: Provide a relative motion visual guide showing how to add velocities when objects move in the same direction (add), opposite direction (subtract), and perpendicular (Pythagorean theorem). Include a subscript-reading guide.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the toy car activity and relative motion problems including the river-crossing scenario.
differentiation.advanced: Solve the general river-crossing problem: determine the heading angle that minimizes crossing time vs. the heading angle that minimizes downstream drift, and explain why these are different.
differentiation.ell: Use physical demonstrations extensively. Provide a visual frame-of-reference diagram with labeled observers. Use color-coded velocity arrows (red = relative to ground, blue = relative to moving object).
differentiation.iep: Focus on 1D relative motion problems first. Provide a visual guide showing 'same direction = add, opposite direction = subtract.' Allow extra time for the 2D river-crossing problem with step-by-step prompts.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how understanding relative motion is essential for air traffic control — a field where diversity and representation matter because controllers make life-and-death decisions. Highlight the contributions of the Tuskegee Airmen, who navigated relative motion challenges during WWII combat missions.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'frame of reference': A passenger on a train sees a tree move backward because___. Two observers can measure different velocities for the same object, but both measurements are correct because___. The river current pushes the boat downstream, so to cross straight the boat must aim___.

vocabulary.definition: A coordinate system or point of view from which motion is observed and measured; motion can appear different from different frames
The velocity of one object as observed from another object; calculated by vector addition of velocities
The frame of reference fixed to the Earth's surface; often the default frame in physics problems
A person or device measuring motion from a particular frame of reference

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: What Is a Frame of Reference?
Section 2: Relative Velocity in One Dimension — Same and Opposite Directions
Section 3: Relative Velocity in Two Dimensions — The River-Crossing Problem
Section 4: Applications of Relative Motion

cer.phenomenon: A commuter on a moving subway train throws a ball straight up and catches it as it comes back down. To the commuter, the ball goes straight up and straight down. But a person standing on the platform outside the train sees the ball travel in a parabolic arc as the train moves past.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the principles of relative motion, I claim that both observers are correct about the ball's path because...
cer.evidence_source: Describe the ball's horizontal and vertical velocity components as seen from each frame of reference (train frame and platform frame).
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because in the train frame, the ball has zero horizontal velocity relative to the thrower, so it appears to go ___. In the platform frame, the ball has the same horizontal velocity as the ___, so it follows a ___. Both descriptions are physically valid because ___.

units.title: Newton's Laws & Forces
units.anchoring_phenomenon: When a city bus brakes suddenly, standing passengers lurch forward even though no one pushes them. Meanwhile, a heavy backpack on the seat slides forward and hits the seat in front. Why do objects of different masses respond differently to the same braking event?
essential_questions: How do forces change the motion of objects?
How can we use free body diagrams to predict an object's acceleration?
What keeps objects moving in a circle, and what happens when that force disappears?
units.crse_theme: Students investigate the physics of forces in culturally relevant contexts — the engineering behind earthquake-resistant buildings in communities of color, the biomechanics of dance forms like breakdancing and ballet, and how Isaac Newton built on the earlier work of scholars from the Islamic Golden Age such as Ibn al-Haytham and Avicenna.

summative: Unit 3 Exam: Forces and Newton's Laws

investigations: Investigation 3: Relationship Between Net Force, Mass, and Acceleration

lessons.title: Newton's First Law — Inertia
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can explain Newton's First Law and predict the motion of an object when the net force acting on it is zero.
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever been in a car that stopped suddenly? What happened to your body? Why did you keep moving even though the car stopped?
lessons.do_now: A hockey puck is sliding on smooth ice with no one touching it. Will it speed up, slow down, or keep the same speed? Explain your reasoning.
materials: Tablecloth and dishes (for tablecloth pull demo)
Coins and index cards (for coin-flick demo)

engage.description: Teacher demonstration: Place a stack of dishes on a tablecloth, then quickly yank the cloth out. The dishes stay in place. Ask: Why didn't the dishes move with the cloth? Then balance a coin on an index card on top of a cup and flick the card sideways — the coin drops straight into the cup. Students explain what they observe.

explore.description: Groups roll toy cars down identical ramps onto different surfaces (sandpaper, felt, smooth tile, waxed surface). They measure how far the car travels on each surface before stopping. Students record data and rank surfaces by friction. Key question: What would happen if there were no friction at all? Would the car ever stop?

explain.description: Present Newton's First Law: An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion at constant velocity, unless acted upon by a net external force. Define inertia as the tendency of an object to resist changes in motion, directly related to mass. Connect to the explore activity: the car on the smooth surface traveled farthest because less friction (less net force) acted on it. In the ideal case of zero friction, the car would never stop.

elaborate.description: Application scenarios: Students predict what happens in each case using Newton's First Law: (1) A passenger in a car that makes a sharp left turn. (2) A book on the dashboard when the car accelerates forward. (3) An astronaut who pushes off a wall inside the International Space Station. Students sketch and explain each scenario.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: Explain why wearing a seatbelt is a direct application of Newton's First Law. Use the terms 'inertia,' 'net force,' and 'constant velocity' in your answer.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a Newton's First Law summary card with key phrases: 'No net force = no change in motion.' Include before/after diagrams for common scenarios (car braking, ball rolling on surfaces).
differentiation.on_level: Complete the surface friction exploration and scenario predictions as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research and present on Aristotle's theory of motion (objects need force to keep moving) and explain why it was wrong. Design an experiment that could be done on the International Space Station to demonstrate Newton's First Law without friction.
differentiation.ell: Use physical demonstrations for every concept. Provide sentence frames: 'The object keeps moving because ___.' 'The net force is zero, so ___.' Include a bilingual vocabulary card with diagrams.
differentiation.iep: Provide a graphic organizer with two columns: 'Net Force = 0' and 'Net Force ≠ 0' with spaces for students to draw and describe what happens in each case. Allow verbal exit ticket responses.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how seatbelt laws emerged from physics understanding of inertia, and how early automotive safety research by engineers like Nils Bohlin (who invented the three-point seatbelt) saved millions of lives. Note how crash safety improvements have historically been slower to reach lower-income communities with older vehicles.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'inertia': A heavy truck is harder to stop than a bicycle because___. Both a moving and a stationary object demonstrate inertia, but___. The passenger was not wearing a seatbelt, so when the car stopped suddenly___.

vocabulary.definition: An object at rest stays at rest and an object in motion stays in motion at constant velocity unless acted upon by a net external force; also called the Law of Inertia
The tendency of an object to resist changes in its state of motion; directly proportional to mass
The vector sum of all forces acting on an object; determines whether the object accelerates
A state in which the net force on an object is zero, resulting in no acceleration; the object is either at rest or moving at constant velocity
A measure of the amount of matter in an object and its resistance to acceleration (inertia); measured in kilograms

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Aristotle vs. Galileo vs. Newton — How Our Understanding of Motion Changed
Section 2: Newton's First Law — The Law of Inertia
Section 3: Inertia and Mass — Why Heavier Objects Are Harder to Accelerate
Section 4: Equilibrium — When Net Force Equals Zero

cer.phenomenon: In a crash test at 48 km/h (about 30 mph), an unbelted crash test dummy continues forward at the car's original speed and strikes the steering wheel with significant force. A belted dummy decelerates with the car and experiences much lower forces. The unbelted dummy's head hits the windshield approximately 0.05 seconds after the car contacts the barrier.
cer.claim_starter: Based on Newton's First Law, I claim that the unbelted dummy continues forward because...
cer.evidence_source: Use the concept of inertia and the time delay (0.05 s) between the car stopping and the dummy hitting the windshield to calculate the distance the dummy traveled inside the car.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because according to Newton's First Law, the dummy's body has inertia and will continue moving at ___ unless a ___ acts on it. The seatbelt provides this force for the belted dummy, but the unbelted dummy's only 'force' is the ___, which is why injuries are so severe.

lessons.title: Newton's Second Law — F = ma
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can apply Newton's Second Law to calculate the net force, mass, or acceleration of an object and explain the relationship between these three quantities.
lessons.circle_prompt: What's easier to push — an empty shopping cart or a full one? A beach ball or a bowling ball? Why? What does this tell us about the relationship between force and mass?
lessons.do_now: Two identical forces push two different objects. Object A has a mass of 2 kg and Object B has a mass of 10 kg. Which object accelerates more? By how much? Show your reasoning.
materials: Dynamics carts and track (1 set per group)
Spring scales or force sensors (1 per group)
Masses (100 g, 200 g, 500 g — sets per group)

engage.description: Show a clip of a race between a sports car and a freight truck, both with the same engine horsepower. Ask: Why does the sports car win? Both have the same force — what's different? Students predict the relationship between force, mass, and acceleration before seeing the equation.

explore.description: Lab investigation: Groups use a dynamics cart on a track.
