Part 1 — Keep mass constant, vary the applied force (1 rubber band, 2 rubber bands, 3 rubber bands), measure acceleration (from distance and time). Part 2 — Keep force constant (same rubber band stretch), vary the mass (add 200 g, 400 g, 600 g), measure acceleration. Groups graph Force vs. Acceleration and Acceleration vs. Mass.

explain.description: Present Newton's Second Law: F_net = ma. Analyze the lab data: Force vs. Acceleration is linear (slope = mass). Acceleration vs. Mass is inverse. Rearrange the equation for each variable: a = F_net/m, m = F_net/a, F_net = ma. Define the unit of force: 1 Newton = 1 kg·m/s^2. Work through three practice problems covering each rearrangement.

elaborate.description: Multi-force problems: A 1500 kg car has an engine force of 4500 N forward and friction of 500 N backward. Students calculate net force and acceleration. Then: What happens to the acceleration if the car picks up 4 passengers (total added mass 300 kg)? Students solve and compare.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A 0.145 kg baseball is pitched at 40 m/s. The batter hits it, and it leaves the bat at 50 m/s in the opposite direction. The bat is in contact with the ball for 0.002 s. Calculate the acceleration and the average force on the ball.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a three-column organizer: 'Find Force → F = ma,' 'Find Acceleration → a = F/m,' 'Find Mass → m = F/a.' Include a worked example for each. Use color-coding for each variable.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the dynamics cart lab and all practice problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Analyze the non-constant force case: What happens when the force depends on position (like a spring)? Explore qualitatively how F = ma still applies at every instant. Calculate the acceleration of a rocket as it burns fuel and loses mass.
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual F = ma triangle (cover the variable you're solving for). Use hands-on lab experience as primary learning before mathematical formalism. Provide bilingual problem glossary.
differentiation.iep: Provide the F = ma triangle on a laminated card. Break multi-step problems into single-step sub-problems. Allow calculator use throughout. Reduce the number of practice problems to focus on one rearrangement at a time.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how Katherine Johnson, a Black mathematician at NASA, used F = ma and related equations to calculate trajectories for the Mercury and Apollo missions. Her hand calculations were so trusted that John Glenn refused to fly until she personally verified the computer's orbital calculations.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'Newton's Second Law': A heavier object has less acceleration when the same force is applied because___. Both a truck and a car experience the same braking force, but___. The net force on the object is 20 N and its mass is 4 kg, so___.

vocabulary.definition: The acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass; F_net = ma
The vector sum of all forces acting on an object; the single force that would produce the same acceleration
The SI unit of force; 1 N = 1 kg·m/s^2; the force needed to accelerate a 1 kg mass at 1 m/s^2
A relationship where one quantity increases as the other increases by the same factor (e.g., double the force → double the acceleration, if mass is constant)
A relationship where one quantity increases as the other decreases by the same factor (e.g., double the mass → half the acceleration, if force is constant)

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Newton's Second Law — The Central Equation of Mechanics
Section 2: F = ma — Three Rearrangements, Three Problem Types
Section 3: The Newton as a Unit of Force
Section 4: Net Force with Multiple Forces Acting

cer.phenomenon: A 70 kg sprinter accelerates from rest to 10 m/s in 1.5 seconds at the start of a race. A 2000 kg car also accelerates from rest to 10 m/s but takes 4.0 seconds.
cer.claim_starter: Based on Newton's Second Law, I claim that the sprinter generates a greater acceleration than the car, but the car requires a greater net force because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the acceleration and net force for both the sprinter and the car using a = Δv/Δt and F = ma.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because while the sprinter's acceleration is ___ m/s^2 compared to the car's ___ m/s^2, the net force on the car (___ N) is much greater than on the sprinter (___ N). This illustrates the role of ___ in Newton's Second Law.

lessons.title: Newton's Third Law and Action-Reaction Pairs
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can identify Newton's Third Law action-reaction force pairs and explain why they do not cancel each other out.
lessons.circle_prompt: If you push against a wall, does the wall push back? How do you know? What evidence do you have?
lessons.do_now: Two ice skaters face each other and push off. Skater A has a mass of 50 kg and Skater B has a mass of 80 kg. Who moves faster after the push? Why? Draw a diagram.
materials: Two spring scales hooked together (1 pair per group)
Two dynamics carts with Velcro or spring bumpers
Skateboards or rolling chairs (2, for teacher demo)

engage.description: Teacher demonstration: Two students sit in rolling chairs facing each other. Student A pushes Student B. Ask: What happens to both students? (Both move apart.) Why does Student A roll backward when they pushed Student B forward? Students discuss in pairs before the formal explanation.

explore.description: Activity 1: Students hook two spring scales together and pull. They observe that both scales always read the same value regardless of who pulls harder or whether one person holds still. Activity 2: Two dynamics carts with a compressed spring between them are released simultaneously. Students compare how far each cart travels for equal masses and unequal masses.

explain.description: Present Newton's Third Law: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. Clarify common misconceptions: (1) Action-reaction pairs act on DIFFERENT objects, so they never cancel. (2) The forces are equal in magnitude even if the objects have different masses — but the accelerations differ because a = F/m. Identify action-reaction pairs in examples: person walking (foot pushes ground backward, ground pushes foot forward), rocket propulsion, swimming.

elaborate.description: Students receive scenario cards and must identify the action-reaction pair for each: (1) A hammer hits a nail. (2) The Earth pulls you down with gravity. (3) A rocket expels exhaust gases. (4) You lean against a wall. For each, students name both forces, what object each acts on, and whether the objects have the same acceleration.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A 1000 kg car rear-ends a 3000 kg truck. According to Newton's Third Law, which vehicle experiences a greater force during the collision? Which experiences greater acceleration? Explain both answers.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a Newton's Third Law template: 'Object A exerts a force on Object B → Object B exerts an equal and opposite force on Object A.' Fill in the blanks for each scenario. Include a common misconception correction sheet.
differentiation.on_level: Complete spring scale activity and scenario card analysis as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Analyze the 'horse and cart' paradox: If the horse pulls the cart with the same force the cart pulls the horse, how does the system ever accelerate? Resolve using free body diagrams for each object separately.
differentiation.ell: Use physical demonstrations for every action-reaction pair. Provide a visual action-reaction pair diagram template with arrows and labels in English and native language. Use consistent color coding (red arrow = action, blue arrow = reaction).
differentiation.iep: Provide a pre-printed list of action-reaction pairs with one force identified and space for the student to fill in the other. Use the spring scale activity as the primary assessment tool. Simplify the exit ticket to multiple choice.

lessons.crse_connection: Explore how rocket propulsion — a direct application of Newton's Third Law — enabled the contributions of Mary Jackson, NASA's first Black female engineer, who worked on wind tunnel experiments that tested how air flows over spacecraft. Discuss how her work required understanding action-reaction forces between air molecules and surfaces.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'action-reaction': When you jump, the ground pushes you up because___. The forces in an action-reaction pair are equal and opposite, but they don't cancel because___. A rocket pushes exhaust gases downward, so___.

vocabulary.definition: For every action force, there is an equal and opposite reaction force; the two forces act on different objects
Two forces that are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and act on different objects as described by Newton's Third Law
The contact force exerted by a surface perpendicular to the object resting on it; the reaction to the object pressing on the surface
The forward force on a rocket or jet produced by expelling mass (exhaust) backward; a Newton's Third Law application

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Newton's Third Law — Action and Reaction
Section 2: Identifying Action-Reaction Pairs
Section 3: Why Action-Reaction Pairs Don't Cancel
Section 4: Applications — Walking, Swimming, Rockets

cer.phenomenon: A 2000 kg SUV collides head-on with a 800 kg compact car. Both drivers report different experiences: the compact car driver is severely injured while the SUV driver walks away with minor bruises. A common misconception is that the SUV exerted a greater force on the compact car than the compact car exerted on the SUV.
cer.claim_starter: Based on Newton's Third Law, I claim that both vehicles experience the same magnitude of force during the collision, but the outcomes differ because...
cer.evidence_source: Apply Newton's Third Law to identify the forces and Newton's Second Law (a = F/m) to calculate the acceleration experienced by each vehicle during the collision.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because Newton's Third Law guarantees the forces are ___, but since the compact car has a ___ mass, it experiences a ___ acceleration (and deceleration), which results in greater injury risk. This is why vehicle safety standards consider ___.

lessons.title: Free Body Diagrams and Net Force Calculations
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can draw a free body diagram showing all forces acting on an object and calculate the net force to predict the object's acceleration.
lessons.circle_prompt: Think of a time when you felt pulled in multiple directions at once — responsibilities, choices, people wanting different things. How did you figure out which way to go? Forces on objects work similarly.
lessons.do_now: A 5 kg box sits on a table. Draw all the forces acting on the box. Are the forces balanced or unbalanced? How do you know?
materials: Free body diagram template sheets (printed, 6 per page)
Toy cars and string for pulling demos

engage.description: Show the sample Regents question from the bungee jumping cluster: 'Which vector diagram correctly models the forces acting on the bungee jumper standing on the platform?' Display the four choices. Ask students to vote before instruction. Reveal that this exact type of question appears on the Regents exam.

explore.description: Scenario stations: Students rotate through four stations, each with a physical setup. Station 1 — A book resting on a table. Station 2 — A mass hanging from a spring scale. Station 3 — A cart being pulled across the table with a string (include friction). Station 4 — A mass hanging from two strings at angles. At each station, students draw a free body diagram and label all forces with arrows proportional to magnitude.

explain.description: Teach the free body diagram procedure: (1) Identify the object. (2) Draw it as a dot. (3) Identify all contact forces (normal, friction, tension, applied) and field forces (gravity). (4) Draw arrows from the dot in the direction of each force, scaled to relative magnitude. (5) Choose a coordinate system. (6) Sum forces in each direction: F_net,x = ΣFx and F_net,y = ΣFy. Work through a horizontal pulling problem and a hanging mass problem.

elaborate.description: Students solve: A 10 kg box is pushed across a floor with 60 N of applied force. Friction is 20 N. (a) Draw the FBD. (b) Calculate the net force. (c) Find the acceleration. (d) If the person stops pushing, what happens? Draw the new FBD and find the new acceleration.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A 3.0 kg object hangs from two ropes. Rope A pulls left at 25 N and upward at 20 N. Rope B pulls right at 25 N and upward at 20 N. Draw the FBD and determine if the object is in equilibrium.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a FBD checklist: 'Did you include gravity? Normal force? Friction? Applied force? Tension?' Include a force identification flowchart. Pre-draw the dot and coordinate axes on templates.
differentiation.on_level: Complete all four stations and net force calculation problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Solve problems involving forces at angles requiring component decomposition. Analyze a system with two connected objects (Atwood machine) using separate FBDs for each object.
differentiation.ell: Use physical setups at each station so students can feel the forces (pull the string, feel the weight). Provide a bilingual force vocabulary card with arrow diagrams. Use color-coding: red = gravity, blue = normal, green = friction, orange = applied.
differentiation.iep: Provide a FBD template with force arrows pre-drawn for common scenarios; students label and calculate magnitudes. Break net force calculation into steps: 'Add all forces pointing right. Add all forces pointing left. Subtract to find net force.' Allow extended time.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how structural engineers use free body diagrams to design bridges and buildings that serve communities. Highlight Fazlur Rahman Khan, a Bangladeshi-American structural engineer who invented the tubular design used in the Willis (Sears) Tower and John Hancock Center, revolutionizing skyscraper construction.
lessons.hochman_activity: Appositive sentences: Students write sentences embedding force definitions. Example: 'The normal force, the perpendicular contact force exerted by a surface, prevents objects from falling through tables and floors.' Students write two more using 'net force' and 'free body diagram.'

vocabulary.definition: A diagram showing a single object as a dot with arrows representing all forces acting on it; arrows point in the direction of each force and are scaled to relative magnitude
A force exerted on an object by a person or another object through direct contact
The force exerted by a surface perpendicular to an object in contact with it; equals mg for an object on a horizontal surface with no other vertical forces
The pulling force transmitted through a string, rope, cable, or wire when it is pulled taut
The force of gravity acting on an object; F_g = mg, directed toward the center of the Earth
The vector sum of all forces acting on an object; F_net = ma

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: What Is a Free Body Diagram and Why Do We Use It?
Section 2: Identifying All Forces on an Object
Section 3: Drawing FBDs — Step-by-Step Procedure
Section 4: Calculating Net Force from an FBD
Section 5: From Net Force to Acceleration — Connecting FBDs to F = ma

cer.phenomenon: An elevator contains a person standing on a bathroom scale. When the elevator is at rest on the ground floor, the scale reads 700 N. As the elevator begins to accelerate upward, the scale reads 840 N. As the elevator moves upward at constant velocity, the scale reads 700 N again. As the elevator decelerates near the top floor, the scale reads 560 N.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the free body diagram analysis, I claim that the scale reading changes because the scale measures the normal force, not the true weight, and this normal force changes when...
cer.evidence_source: Draw a free body diagram for the person during each phase (at rest, accelerating up, constant velocity, decelerating). Calculate the net force and acceleration in each case.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because when the elevator accelerates upward, the normal force must be ___ than the weight to produce a net ___ force, making the scale read ___. When decelerating, the net force is ___, so the normal force is ___ than the weight.

lessons.title: Weight, Mass, and the Force of Gravity
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can distinguish between mass and weight, calculate the weight of an object using F_g = mg, and explain how weight changes with location while mass stays constant.
lessons.circle_prompt: If you could visit any planet or moon in the solar system, where would you go? Would you weigh more or less there? Would you have more or less mass?
lessons.do_now: A 70 kg astronaut stands on Earth where g = 9.81 m/s^2. Calculate their weight. Then calculate their weight on the Moon where g = 1.62 m/s^2. Did their mass change?

engage.description: Show a clip of astronauts on the International Space Station floating and 'weightless.' Ask: Have the astronauts lost mass? Have they lost weight? Are they truly weightless? (They are in free fall — the ISS and astronauts fall together, so there is no normal force, creating the sensation of weightlessness.) Students discuss the surprising answer.

explore.description: Students measure the same object's mass on a triple-beam balance (in grams/kg) and its weight on a spring scale (in Newtons). They do this for five objects of different mass. They plot Weight (N) vs. Mass (kg) on graph paper. The slope of the line should be approximately 9.81 — students calculate it and recognize this as g.

explain.description: Define weight: F_g = mg, where g is the gravitational field strength (9.81 N/kg on Earth). Mass is intrinsic (amount of matter, in kg) and does not change with location. Weight is a force (in N) and changes depending on the local value of g. Demonstrate: the same 1 kg mass weighs 9.81 N on Earth, 1.62 N on the Moon, and 24.79 N on Jupiter. Complete a 'Weight on Other Worlds' table as a class.

elaborate.description: Students calculate their own weight on Earth, the Moon, Mars, and Jupiter using the planetary gravity data card. Then they solve: An object weighs 50 N on Earth. What is its mass? What would it weigh on Mars (g = 3.71 m/s^2)? If you wanted an object to weigh 100 N on Mars, what mass would it need?

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) What is the mass of an object that weighs 196 N on Earth? (2) Would this object have the same mass on the Moon? (3) Would it have the same weight? Calculate its weight on the Moon (g = 1.62 m/s^2).

differentiation.approaching: Provide a Mass vs. Weight comparison chart with fill-in blanks. Pre-organize the 'Weight on Other Worlds' table with formulas visible. Include a conversion helper: 'To find weight from mass, multiply by g.'
differentiation.on_level: Complete the graphing lab and planetary weight calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research why g varies slightly at different locations on Earth (altitude, latitude, local geology). Calculate how much their weight changes between sea level and the top of Mount Everest.
differentiation.ell: Use visual weight vs. mass comparison posters with images of scales (spring scale = weight in N, balance = mass in kg). Provide sentence frames for explaining the difference. Include native language vocabulary cards.
differentiation.iep: Provide a Weight = mass x g card with examples. Use a simple two-step template for all problems: 'Step 1: Identify mass and g. Step 2: Multiply.' Reduce the planetary calculations to two planets. Allow calculator use throughout.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how understanding weight vs. mass is critical for space missions, including the contributions of Dr. Mae Jemison, the first African American woman in space, who conducted experiments on weightlessness and bone loss aboard the Space Shuttle Endeavour in 1992.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'weight' and 'mass': An astronaut on the Moon can jump higher than on Earth because___. Mass and weight are related, but they are not the same thing because___. The gravitational field strength on Jupiter is 24.79 m/s^2, so a 50 kg person would weigh___.

vocabulary.definition: The gravitational force acting on an object; F_g = mg; a vector quantity measured in Newtons directed toward the center of the attracting body
The quantity of matter in an object; an intrinsic property measured in kilograms that does not change with location
The force of gravity per unit mass at a given location; on Earth's surface, g = 9.81 N/kg (equivalent to 9.81 m/s^2)
The normal force experienced by an object, which can differ from true weight when the object is accelerating (e.g., in an elevator or on a roller coaster)
The condition in which an object experiences no normal force; occurs during free fall, not due to the absence of gravity

Section 2: Calculating Weight Using F_g = mg
Section 3: Weight on Other Worlds — How g Changes
Section 4: Apparent Weight and Weightlessness

cer.phenomenon: A produce company ships fruit from Earth to a hypothetical Moon colony. On Earth, they pack 100 kg of apples into a crate. A customer on the Moon colony weighs the crate on a spring scale and reads only 162 N, which corresponds to 16.5 kg on Earth. The customer claims they were shortchanged. The company insists they shipped 100 kg.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the difference between mass and weight, I claim that both the company and the customer can be correct because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the weight of 100 kg of apples on the Moon (g = 1.62 m/s^2) and explain why a spring scale calibrated for Earth would give a misleading reading on the Moon.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because a spring scale measures ___, not mass. On the Moon, 100 kg has a weight of only ___ N, which a scale calibrated for Earth would incorrectly report as ___ kg. To accurately measure mass on the Moon, the customer should use a ___ instead.

lessons.title: Friction — Static and Kinetic
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can distinguish between static and kinetic friction, calculate friction forces using Ff = mu * F_N, and predict how friction affects the motion of objects.
lessons.circle_prompt: What surfaces are the most slippery you have ever walked on? What made them slippery? What did you do differently to walk safely?
lessons.do_now: A 10 kg box sits on a rough floor. You push it with 20 N of force and it does not move. Then you push with 40 N and it starts sliding. What was the maximum static friction? Is kinetic friction larger or smaller than static friction?
materials: Wooden blocks with different surfaces (smooth, rough, sandpaper-covered)
Masses to place on blocks (200 g, 500 g, 1 kg)
Various surface materials (glass, cardboard, rubber mat, wax paper)

engage.description: Show a video of curling — the sport where players slide a stone across ice and sweepers brush the ice ahead of it. Ask: Why do they sweep? What effect does sweeping have on friction? How can changing friction change the outcome of the game? This introduces friction as something that can be measured and manipulated.

explore.description: Lab investigation: Students pull a wooden block at constant speed across different surfaces using a spring scale to measure kinetic friction force. They vary the normal force by adding masses on top of the block. Students create a data table of F_friction vs. F_normal for each surface and graph the results. The slope of each line is the coefficient of kinetic friction (mu_k).

explain.description: Define friction: a contact force that opposes the relative motion (or attempted motion) between surfaces. Static friction (Ff <= mu_s * F_N) prevents motion and adjusts up to a maximum. Kinetic friction (Ff = mu_k * F_N) acts on sliding objects and is constant. Key relationships: mu_s > mu_k for the same surfaces; friction depends on normal force and surface type, NOT on surface area. Connect to lab data.

elaborate.description: Multi-step problem: A 20 kg box is pushed across a floor (mu_k = 0.30) with a force of 100 N horizontally. Students draw the FBD, calculate F_N (= mg = 196 N), kinetic friction (= 0.30 x 196 = 58.8 N), net force (= 100 - 58.8 = 41.2 N), and acceleration (= 41.2/20 = 2.06 m/s^2). Then: What minimum force is needed to start the box moving if mu_s = 0.40?

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A 5.0 kg block slides across a surface with mu_k = 0.25. (a) Calculate the friction force. (b) If the block has an initial velocity of 4.0 m/s, what is its acceleration? (c) How far does it slide before stopping?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a friction force calculation template: 'Step 1: Find F_N (usually = mg for horizontal surfaces). Step 2: Multiply mu x F_N.' Include a static vs. kinetic friction comparison chart with visuals.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the friction lab and multi-step problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Investigate how friction depends on speed (it doesn't for simple kinetic friction, but does for drag in fluids). Calculate the coefficient of friction for a car skidding to a stop from known speed and stopping distance.
differentiation.ell: Use physical demonstrations — students feel the difference between static and kinetic friction by starting to push a heavy book. Provide bilingual friction vocabulary with diagrams showing force directions.
differentiation.iep: Provide a laminated Ff = mu * F_N reference card. Break multi-step friction problems into numbered single-step parts. Reduce practice problems. Allow use of calculator and formula card for exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how understanding friction is crucial for tire design in different communities and climates. Explore how engineers design tires for different conditions (rain, snow, off-road) and how access to proper tires is a safety equity issue in communities with harsh winters.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'friction': Static friction is greater than kinetic friction because___. Friction depends on the normal force and the coefficient of friction, but it does not depend on surface area, so___. The ice was very smooth with a low coefficient of friction, so the hockey puck___.

vocabulary.definition: A contact force that opposes the relative motion or attempted motion between two surfaces in contact
The friction force that prevents an object from starting to move; adjustable up to a maximum value of Ff = mu_s * F_N
The constant friction force acting on an object that is already sliding; Ff = mu_k * F_N
A dimensionless number that characterizes the roughness between two surfaces; higher values mean more friction
The perpendicular contact force exerted by a surface on an object; on a horizontal surface with no other vertical forces, F_N = mg

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: What Causes Friction? — Surface Interactions at the Microscopic Level
Section 2: Static vs. Kinetic Friction
Section 3: Calculating Friction — Ff = mu * F_N
Section 4: Friction in Free Body Diagrams and Net Force Problems

cer.phenomenon: On a dry road, a car traveling at 25 m/s can stop in approximately 32 m. On a wet road, the same car at the same speed requires approximately 64 m to stop. On an icy road, the stopping distance increases to approximately 160 m. The car's mass and brakes are identical in all three cases.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the relationship between friction and stopping distance, I claim that road conditions primarily affect stopping distance by changing...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the coefficient of kinetic friction for each road condition using the kinematic equation vf^2 = vi^2 + 2ad and F_friction = mu * mg.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because the coefficient of friction decreases from approximately ___ (dry) to ___ (wet) to ___ (icy), which reduces the ___ force and therefore reduces the ___, resulting in a longer stopping distance.

lessons.title: Inclined Planes
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can resolve gravitational force into components parallel and perpendicular to an inclined plane and calculate the acceleration of an object on a frictionless or frictional incline.
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever tried to walk up or push something up a steep hill? What made it harder as the hill got steeper? At what angle would it become impossible?
lessons.do_now: A 5 kg block sits on a ramp tilted at 30 degrees. Draw the force of gravity straight down. Now try to split that gravity arrow into two parts: one along the ramp and one into the ramp surface. Which part tries to slide the block down?

engage.description: Show images of San Francisco's steepest streets (grades up to 31.5%) and ask: Why do cars sometimes slide on these streets? What forces are acting? Then show a video of a truck failing to climb an icy hill. Ask: What angle would make it impossible for any vehicle to climb, even without ice?

explore.description: Groups place a wooden block on an adjustable ramp and slowly increase the angle until the block begins to slide. They measure this critical angle (angle of repose). Then they set the ramp to 20, 30, and 40 degrees and use a spring scale to measure the force needed to hold the block stationary on the ramp at each angle. Students note the pattern: steeper angle → more force needed.

explain.description: Teach the inclined plane force decomposition: gravity splits into F_parallel = mg sin(theta) along the ramp and F_perpendicular = mg cos(theta) into the surface. The normal force equals F_perpendicular (not mg!). For a frictionless incline: a = g sin(theta). With friction: a = g sin(theta) - mu_k * g cos(theta). Draw the full FBD on the incline with rotated coordinate axes. Work through a complete example: 8 kg block on a 37-degree incline with mu_k = 0.20.

elaborate.description: Students solve: A 50 kg skier starts from rest at the top of a 25-degree slope that is 100 m long. If mu_k = 0.10, what is the skier's acceleration? How fast are they going at the bottom? How long does the run take?

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A 4.0 kg block is on a frictionless 30-degree incline. (a) What is F_parallel? (b) What is F_perpendicular? (c) What is the normal force? (d) What is the acceleration down the ramp?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a color-coded inclined plane FBD template: red arrow for gravity (straight down), green for F_parallel (along ramp, downhill), blue for F_perpendicular (into surface), purple for normal force (out of surface). Include the formulas next to each arrow.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the ramp exploration and incline calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Determine the angle at which the block begins to slide and use it to calculate the coefficient of static friction (tan(theta_c) = mu_s). Analyze a block being pushed UP an incline against both gravity and friction.
differentiation.ell: Use the physical ramp extensively before introducing equations. Provide step-by-step visual guides showing how to decompose the gravity vector. Label diagrams in English and native language.
differentiation.iep: Provide a pre-drawn inclined plane FBD with forces labeled and formulas written next to each. Break problems into: 'Step 1: Find F_parallel. Step 2: Find F_perpendicular. Step 3: Find normal force. Step 4: Find friction. Step 5: Find net force. Step 6: Find acceleration.' Allow calculator use throughout.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how the ancient Egyptians used inclined planes (ramps) to build the pyramids, and how the Inca built steep road systems through the Andes mountains with switchback ramps. Both civilizations understood intuitively that ramps reduce the force needed to move heavy objects — the same physics students calculate today.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'inclined plane': The component of gravity along the ramp increases as the angle increases because___. Both F_parallel and F_perpendicular come from gravity, but they act in different directions, so___. The ramp angle was increased from 20 to 40 degrees, so the block's acceleration___.

vocabulary.definition: A flat surface tilted at an angle to the horizontal; one of the simple machines that allows analysis of forces in components
The component of gravitational force directed along (parallel to) the surface of an inclined plane; causes the object to accelerate down the ramp
The component of gravitational force directed into (perpendicular to) the surface of an inclined plane; balanced by the normal force
The maximum angle at which an object on a surface remains stationary; at this angle, the component of gravity along the ramp equals the maximum static friction force

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Why Inclined Planes Require a Rotated Coordinate System
Section 2: Decomposing Gravity — F_parallel and F_perpendicular
Section 3: Normal Force on an Incline (F_N = mg cos theta, NOT mg)
Section 4: Acceleration on a Frictionless Incline
Section 5: Acceleration on an Incline with Friction

cer.phenomenon: A moving company must slide a 200 kg piano down a ramp from a second-floor apartment. The ramp is 6 m long and the second floor is 3 m above the ground (30-degree angle). Without friction, the piano would accelerate dangerously. They lay a carpet on the ramp (mu_k = 0.45) and the piano slides down slowly and controllably.
cer.claim_starter: Based on inclined plane analysis, I claim that the carpet reduces the piano's acceleration to a safe level because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the acceleration of the piano without friction (a = g sin 30) and with friction (a = g sin 30 - mu_k * g cos 30). Compare both values and calculate the piano's speed at the bottom in each case.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because without friction the acceleration would be ___ m/s^2, reaching a speed of ___ m/s at the bottom, but with the carpet's friction the acceleration is reduced to ___ m/s^2, resulting in a manageable speed of ___ m/s.

lessons.title: Circular Motion and Centripetal Force
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can explain that an object moving in a circle is accelerating, identify the centripetal force keeping it in circular motion, and calculate centripetal acceleration and force.
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever been on a merry-go-round, a spinning ride at an amusement park, or taken a sharp turn in a car? What did you feel? Which direction were you pulled?
lessons.do_now: Tie a small object to a string and swing it in a horizontal circle above your head. If you let go of the string, which direction does the object fly — outward, inward, or tangent to the circle? Try it (safely) and observe.
materials: Small masses on strings (1 per student, for safe spinning)
Rubber stoppers and glass tubes for centripetal force apparatus (1 per group)

engage.description: Show a video of a car making a sharp turn — a coffee cup on the dashboard slides to the outside of the turn. Ask: What force pushes the cup outward? (Trick question — no force pushes it outward! The cup continues in a straight line due to inertia while the car turns underneath it. The cup appears to slide outward from the car's frame of reference.) This challenges the common 'centrifugal force' misconception.

explore.description: Lab activity: Students swing a rubber stopper in a horizontal circle using the centripetal force apparatus (stopper on string through a glass tube, with hanging masses providing the centripetal force). They vary the radius (string length) and the speed (number of revolutions per time) and observe how the hanging mass needed to maintain circular motion changes. Students record data on force, radius, and period.

explain.description: Define centripetal acceleration: ac = v^2/r, always directed toward the center of the circle. Centripetal force: Fc = mac = mv^2/r, also toward the center. Emphasize: centripetal force is not a new type of force — it is the name for whatever force provides the center-directed acceleration (tension, gravity, friction, normal force). Examples: the Moon orbits Earth (gravity is centripetal force), a car turns (friction is centripetal force), a ball on a string (tension is centripetal force).

elaborate.description: Problem: A 1000 kg car makes a turn on a flat road with radius 50 m at 15 m/s. (a) What centripetal acceleration does the car experience? (b) What centripetal force is needed? (c) What provides this force? (friction) (d) What is the minimum coefficient of friction needed? Students solve and discuss what happens if mu is too low (the car skids outward).

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A 0.50 kg ball on a 1.2 m string is swung in a horizontal circle at 4.0 m/s. (a) What is the centripetal acceleration? (b) What is the tension in the string (centripetal force)? (c) If the string breaks, describe the path of the ball.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a circular motion reference card: 'Centripetal = toward center. Centrifugal = not real (just inertia).' Include the formulas ac = v^2/r and Fc = mv^2/r with labeled diagrams. Pre-identify the centripetal force in each example.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the centripetal force lab and calculation problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Analyze the forces on a car going over a hill (reduced normal force) and through a valley (increased normal force). Calculate the speed at which a car would become airborne at the top of a hill of known radius.
differentiation.ell: Use the physical spinning activity extensively. Provide diagrams with arrows showing the direction of velocity (tangent), acceleration (toward center), and the force providing centripetal acceleration. Label all diagrams bilingually.
differentiation.iep: Focus on the concept that centripetal force always points toward the center. Provide a simplified formula card. Break problems into: 'Step 1: Identify the center. Step 2: Identify what force points toward the center. Step 3: Calculate using Fc = mv^2/r.' Reduce practice problems.

lessons.crse_connection: Explore the physics of centrifuges, which are critical in medical laboratories for separating blood components. Discuss how access to centrifuge technology in clinics serving underserved communities — and the physics-based innovation of hand-powered 'paperfuge' centrifuges developed for low-resource settings — can improve healthcare equity.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'centripetal': An object moving in a circle is accelerating because___. People often say they feel pushed outward on a spinning ride, but there is no outward force acting on them because___. The car entered the turn too fast for the available friction, so___.

vocabulary.definition: The acceleration directed toward the center of a circular path; ac = v^2/r; responsible for changing the direction of velocity
The net force directed toward the center of a circular path that keeps an object moving in a circle; Fc = mv^2/r; not a new type of force but a role played by existing forces
The instantaneous velocity of an object moving in a circle, directed tangent to the circular path at any point
The time for one complete revolution around a circular path; related to speed by v = 2*pi*r/T
A fictitious (non-real) outward force felt in a rotating reference frame; actually the result of inertia, not a real force

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: What Is Circular Motion? — Constant Speed, Changing Direction
Section 2: Centripetal Acceleration — Always Toward the Center
Section 3: Centripetal Force — What Provides It?
Section 4: Calculations — ac = v^2/r and Fc = mv^2/r
Section 5: What Happens When the Force Disappears?

cer.phenomenon: On a loop-the-loop roller coaster, the track has a radius of 10 m at the top of the loop. A 60 kg rider feels 'light' at the top and 'heavy' at the bottom. At a certain minimum speed, the rider feels completely weightless at the top of the loop. Below this speed, the coaster would fall off the track.
cer.claim_starter: Based on centripetal force analysis, I claim that the minimum speed at the top of the loop must be approximately ___ m/s because...
cer.evidence_source: At the top of the loop, both gravity and normal force point toward the center. At the minimum speed, the normal force is zero and gravity alone provides the centripetal force: mg = mv^2/r. Solve for v.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because at the minimum speed, gravity provides ___ the centripetal force needed (F_N = 0), so mg = mv^2/r simplifies to v = sqrt(___). For r = 10 m, v = ___ m/s. Below this speed, gravity provides ___ centripetal force than needed and the rider would fall away from the track.

lessons.title: Applications — Elevators, Pulleys, and Connected Objects
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can analyze systems with multiple connected objects using free body diagrams and Newton's Second Law to calculate tension, acceleration, and apparent weight.
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever felt heavier or lighter in an elevator? When — going up, going down, starting, or stopping? Could you explain why that happens?
lessons.do_now: You stand on a scale in an elevator. The scale reads 700 N when the elevator is at rest. Predict: Will the scale read more, less, or the same when the elevator (a) accelerates upward? (b) moves up at constant speed? (c) decelerates while going up?
materials: Pulley systems (single and double, 1 per group)
String and masses (50 g, 100 g, 200 g, 500 g)

engage.description: Show a video of an elevator scale experiment: a person stands on a bathroom scale inside a glass elevator and the reading changes as the elevator starts, moves, and stops. Display the scale readings during each phase. Ask: When does the person weigh the most? The least? Are they actually gaining and losing mass?

explore.description: Pulley lab: Groups set up an Atwood machine (two different masses connected by a string over a pulley). They predict which mass will accelerate downward and measure the actual acceleration (from distance and time). They compare to the theoretical prediction: a = (m1 - m2)g / (m1 + m2). Groups try different mass combinations and test the formula.

explain.description: Teach the system approach: (1) Draw separate FBDs for each object. (2) Write Newton's Second Law for each object. (3) Note that connected objects have the same magnitude of acceleration and the string has the same tension throughout. Work through the Atwood machine derivation. Then the elevator problem: FBD for a person on a scale shows F_N (up, which is the scale reading) and F_g (down). Apply F_net = ma: F_N - mg = ma, so F_N = m(g + a). When a is positive (upward acceleration), apparent weight increases.

elaborate.description: Connected objects on a table: A 3 kg block on a frictionless table is connected by a string over a pulley to a 2 kg hanging block. Students draw FBDs for both objects, set up equations, and solve for acceleration and tension. Then: What changes if the table has friction (mu_k = 0.20)?

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A 60 kg person stands on a scale in an elevator accelerating downward at 2.0 m/s^2. (a) Draw the FBD. (b) Calculate the scale reading (apparent weight). (c) Compare to their actual weight.

differentiation.approaching: Provide separate FBD templates for each object in the system with arrows pre-drawn. Include a step-by-step guide for the Atwood machine: 'Write F_net = ma for each mass. The heavier mass accelerates down. Tension is the same in both equations.'
differentiation.on_level: Complete the Atwood machine lab and elevator/pulley problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Analyze a three-mass Atwood machine or a system with a pulley on an incline. Determine the mass ratio needed for equilibrium in each system.
differentiation.ell: Use physical pulley setups to demonstrate before calculating. Provide visual guides showing FBDs for elevator scenarios with up/down arrows clearly labeled. Use color-coding for different forces in each FBD.
differentiation.iep: Provide a pre-written Atwood machine formula: a = (m1 - m2)g / (m1 + m2). Focus on plug-and-chug calculations. Break the elevator problem into 3 steps with blanks: 'Step 1: Identify forces. Step 2: F_N - mg = ma. Step 3: Solve for F_N.' Allow extended time.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the history of elevators and their role in urban development — how Elisha Otis's safety elevator made skyscrapers possible, and how Alexander Miles, a Black inventor, patented automatic elevator doors in 1887, making elevators safer for everyone. Connect to how understanding forces in elevator systems is still essential for modern engineering.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'tension' and 'apparent weight': The tension in the string is the same on both sides of the pulley because___. A person in a downward-accelerating elevator feels lighter, but their mass hasn't changed because___. The heavier mass in an Atwood machine accelerates downward, so the lighter mass accelerates___.

vocabulary.definition: A system of two masses connected by a string over a frictionless pulley; used to study Newton's Second Law with connected objects
The normal force experienced by a person, which differs from true weight when the person is accelerating; what a scale reads
A group of objects analyzed together; connected objects in a system share the same acceleration magnitude
The pulling force in a string or rope; in an ideal (massless, non-stretchy) string, tension is the same throughout
A simple machine that redirects the direction of a tension force; an ideal pulley is frictionless and massless

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Connected Objects — Same String, Same Tension, Same Acceleration
Section 2: The Atwood Machine — Deriving the Acceleration Formula
Section 3: Elevator Problems — Apparent Weight and Acceleration
Section 4: Objects on Tables Connected to Hanging Masses

cer.phenomenon: A hospital elevator carries a patient on a gurney with medical monitoring equipment that measures vital signs. The patient's monitored 'weight' fluctuates during the elevator ride: it reads higher than normal when the elevator starts going up, normal during constant-speed travel, and lower than normal as the elevator slows near the destination floor.
cer.claim_starter: Based on Newton's Second Law, I claim that the patient's monitored weight changes because the scale measures normal force, which depends on...
cer.evidence_source: Draw FBDs and apply F_net = ma for each phase of the elevator ride (starting, constant speed, stopping). Calculate the apparent weight for a 70 kg patient during upward acceleration of 1.5 m/s^2 and deceleration of -1.5 m/s^2.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because during upward acceleration, F_N = m(g + a) = ___ N (heavier), during constant velocity, F_N = mg = ___ N (normal), and during deceleration, F_N = m(g - a) = ___ N (lighter). The patient's actual mass of ___ kg never changes.

lessons.title: Forces Unit Review and Problem-Solving Strategies
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can apply Newton's Laws to multi-step problems involving forces, friction, inclines, and circular motion, selecting the correct approach and justifying my reasoning.
lessons.circle_prompt: What's the most challenging problem you have solved so far this year — in physics or in life? What strategy helped you work through it? What did you learn about yourself as a problem solver?
lessons.do_now: Quick categorization: For each scenario, state which type of problem it is (equilibrium, F=ma on flat surface, incline, circular motion, connected objects) and which equations you would use: (1) A box slides down a ramp. (2) Two masses on an Atwood machine. (3) A car rounds a curve. (4) A crate is pushed at constant velocity across a floor.
materials: Review problem set (tiered, 20 problems across all topics)
Whiteboard markers and large whiteboards (1 per group)

engage.description: Present a Regents-style question cluster: A delivery person pushes a 30 kg cart up a 15-degree ramp into a truck. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.25. Ask: How many different physics concepts from this unit do you need to solve this problem? Students brainstorm a list (inclined plane decomposition, friction, Newton's Second Law, FBD) and realize that real problems combine multiple concepts.

explore.description: Gallery walk problem-solving: Six problems are posted around the room on large whiteboards, each requiring a different combination of skills (1: equilibrium FBD, 2: F=ma with friction, 3: incline without friction, 4: incline with friction, 5: circular motion, 6: Atwood machine). Groups rotate to each station, add one step of the solution, and move on. By the end, each problem is solved collaboratively.

explain.description: Whole-class review of the gallery walk solutions. Teacher highlights common errors: forgetting to use mg cos(theta) for normal force on inclines, confusing mass and weight, using the wrong equation for circular motion, sign errors. Present a universal problem-solving framework: (1) Read and visualize. (2) Draw FBD. (3) Choose coordinate system. (4) Write F_net = ma in each direction. (5) Substitute known values. (6) Solve. (7) Check units and reasonableness.

elaborate.description: Challenge problem combining multiple concepts: A 5 kg box on a 30-degree ramp (mu_k = 0.20) is connected by a string over a pulley to a 3 kg hanging mass. Which direction does the system accelerate? Find the acceleration and the tension. Students must combine incline, friction, and connected-object analysis.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A 0.80 kg ball on a 0.50 m string swings in a vertical circle. At the top of the circle, the tension in the string is 5.0 N. What is the speed of the ball at the top? (Hint: At the top, both tension and gravity point toward the center.)

differentiation.approaching: Provide a problem-type identification guide: 'If the object is on a ramp → incline problem. If the object moves in a circle → centripetal force. If objects are connected → system analysis.' Include the universal solving framework as a laminated card.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the gallery walk and work through the tiered review problem set covering all force types.
differentiation.advanced: Solve the ramp-pulley combination problem and analyze a banked curve (no friction needed). Derive the relationship between banking angle and speed for a frictionless banked turn.
differentiation.ell: Pair ELL students with strong problem-solvers during the gallery walk. Provide a problem-type visual dictionary with diagrams and key equations for each type. Allow reference to all materials during practice.
differentiation.iep: Provide a condensed review focusing on the three most common problem types (flat surface with friction, free fall, and one incline problem). Break each into a numbered checklist. Allow all references during practice. Reduce total problem count.

lessons.crse_connection: Highlight how understanding forces is essential for prosthetic design — engineers use FBDs and Newton's Laws to design artificial limbs. Discuss how Van Phillips, inspired by the cheetah's leg, designed the Flex-Foot running prosthetic that enabled Paralympic athletes to compete at the highest levels, democratizing athletic achievement.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences integrating multiple force concepts: An object on a ramp accelerates because___. A car can safely turn on a flat road, but if the turn is too sharp or the speed too high, the car skids because___. The system's acceleration depends on the total net force and total mass, so adding mass to the Atwood machine___.

vocabulary.definition: A condition where the net force on an object is zero (F_net = 0); the object has zero acceleration (at rest or constant velocity)
Equilibrium while the object is moving at constant velocity; net force is still zero
Equilibrium while the object is at rest; net force is zero and velocity is zero
A simplified diagram showing all forces acting on a single object as arrows from a central point; the essential first step in solving any force problem
The vector sum of all forces on an object; determines whether the object accelerates and in which direction

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Universal Problem-Solving Framework for Force Problems
Section 2: Review — Identifying the Problem Type
Section 3: Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
Section 4: Combining Multiple Concepts in One Problem

cer.phenomenon: A 1200 kg car approaches a hill that curves over the top with a radius of 40 m. The speed limit sign says 50 km/h (13.9 m/s). A physics student claims that if a car goes too fast over the top of the hill, the tires will lose contact with the road. The student calculates that at 72 km/h (20 m/s) the car would become airborne.
cer.claim_starter: Based on Newton's Second Law and centripetal motion analysis, I claim that the car becomes airborne at the top of the hill when the speed exceeds ___ m/s because...
cer.evidence_source: At the top of the hill, the centripetal acceleration is directed downward (toward the center of the circular arc). The forces acting on the car are gravity (down) and normal force (up). Apply F_net = mac: mg - F_N = mv^2/r. The car becomes airborne when F_N = 0.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because when F_N = 0, the equation becomes mg = mv^2/r, giving v = sqrt(gr) = sqrt(___ x ___) = ___ m/s. Above this speed, gravity alone cannot provide enough centripetal force, so the car ___ the road. This explains why speed limits on hilly roads account for ___.

units.title: Momentum & Impulse
units.anchoring_phenomenon: In a car crash at 50 km/h, an unbelted driver hitting a rigid steering wheel experiences forces that can be fatal. An airbag increases the time of the collision by a factor of 10 and reduces the peak force by a factor of 10. How can changing the time of a collision so dramatically change the outcome?
essential_questions: How do impulse and momentum explain what happens during collisions?
Why is the total momentum of a system conserved when no external forces act?
How can we design devices that reduce the force experienced during collisions?
units.crse_theme: Students investigate how momentum and impulse principles are applied in safety engineering across communities — from helmet design for cyclists in urban neighborhoods to the physics of martial arts (breaking boards in karate, redirecting force in aikido), connecting diverse cultural practices to physics principles.

summative: Investigation: Conservation of Momentum with Colliding Carts

investigations: Investigation 4: Conservation of Momentum in Collisions

lessons.title: Momentum — The Measure of Motion
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can calculate the momentum of an object and explain why momentum depends on both mass and velocity.
lessons.circle_prompt: Which would be harder to stop — a truck moving slowly or a bicycle moving fast? What about the truck and bicycle moving at the same speed? What factors matter when trying to stop something?
lessons.do_now: A 0.145 kg baseball traveling at 40 m/s and a 7.0 kg bowling ball traveling at 2.0 m/s both head toward you. Which one has more momentum? Which one would you rather try to catch? Why might your answers differ?
materials: Various balls (tennis, baseball, basketball, bowling ball — or equivalent masses)

engage.description: Show a side-by-side comparison: a ping-pong ball fired at 1000 m/s vs. a bowling ball rolling at 1 m/s. Which has more momentum? Students calculate both (p = mv) and are surprised that the bowling ball's momentum (7 x 1 = 7 kg·m/s) far exceeds the ping-pong ball's (0.0027 x 1000 = 2.7 kg·m/s). This introduces momentum as the quantity that combines mass AND velocity.

explore.description: Groups rank 8 objects by momentum: (1) a 1500 kg car at 30 m/s, (2) a 100 kg sprinter at 10 m/s, (3) a 0.058 kg tennis ball at 60 m/s, (4) a 0.145 kg baseball at 40 m/s, (5) a 7.26 kg shot put at 14 m/s, (6) a 0.005 kg bullet at 900 m/s, (7) an 80 kg person walking at 1.5 m/s, (8) a 75,000 kg loaded semi-truck at 25 m/s. Students calculate, rank, and discuss which they would least want to be hit by and why 'most momentum' doesn't always mean 'most dangerous.'

explain.description: Define momentum: p = mv, a vector quantity with the same direction as velocity, measured in kg·m/s. Key properties: momentum is proportional to both mass and velocity, it has a direction, and changing momentum requires a force over time (preview of impulse). Show that Newton originally wrote his Second Law as F = Δp/Δt (rate of change of momentum), not F = ma. Work through examples including a direction change: a ball bouncing off a wall.

elaborate.description: Direction matters problem: A 0.4 kg ball moves east at 10 m/s and bounces off a wall, returning west at 8 m/s. Calculate the change in momentum. (Students must recognize that the direction change means Δp = p_final - p_initial = (-3.2) - (4.0) = -7.2 kg·m/s, not 0.8.) Discuss why this is larger than if the ball simply stopped.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A 70 kg hockey player skates north at 8 m/s. (a) What is the player's momentum? (b) A 90 kg player skates south at 6 m/s. What is their momentum? (c) Which player has greater momentum magnitude? (d) If they collide head-on, what is the total momentum of the system?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a momentum calculation template: p = m x v, with units clearly shown (kg x m/s = kg·m/s). Include a direction reminder: 'Momentum is a vector — include direction.' Pre-set up the ranking activity with a calculation table.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the momentum ranking activity and direction-change problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research and present on the concept of momentum in special relativity (relativistic momentum) and explain why objects cannot reach the speed of light.
differentiation.ell: Use physical demonstrations with rolling balls of different masses and speeds. Provide a visual momentum comparison chart with bar diagrams. Include bilingual vocabulary and sentence frames.
differentiation.iep: Provide a p = mv reference card with worked examples. Focus on magnitude calculations before introducing direction. Reduce the ranking activity to 5 objects. Allow calculator use throughout.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how understanding momentum is essential in sports analysis — from cricket bowling speeds to NFL tackle physics. Highlight how Dr. Stefan Duma, a biomechanical engineer, uses momentum calculations to design safer football helmets, and how recent research has focused on protecting youth athletes in underserved communities where outdated equipment is common.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'momentum': A loaded truck is harder to stop than an empty one traveling at the same speed because___. A bullet and a bowling ball can have the same momentum, but the bullet travels much faster because___. The ball bounced off the wall and reversed direction, so the change in momentum was ___ than if it had simply stopped.

vocabulary.definition: The product of an object's mass and velocity; p = mv; a vector quantity measured in kg·m/s that describes the 'quantity of motion'
The difference between final and initial momentum; Delta p = p_final - p_initial; accounts for changes in both speed and direction
A system with no external net forces acting on it; the total momentum of an isolated system is conserved
A quantity with both magnitude and direction; momentum, like velocity, is a vector and direction must be included in all calculations

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: What Is Momentum? — The Product of Mass and Velocity
Section 2: Calculating Momentum and Its Units
Section 3: Momentum as a Vector — Direction Matters
Section 4: Change in Momentum — Why Bouncing Has Greater Delta p Than Stopping

cer.phenomenon: In bowling, a 7.26 kg ball traveling at 8.0 m/s strikes a 1.5 kg pin at rest. After the collision, the pin flies backward at 12 m/s while the ball continues forward at a reduced speed. A common misconception is that the lighter pin must have less momentum than the heavier ball.
cer.claim_starter: Based on momentum calculations, I claim that the pin's momentum after the collision is ___ compared to the ball's change in momentum because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the ball's initial momentum, the pin's final momentum, and the ball's change in momentum. Compare the magnitudes.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because the pin's momentum after the collision (p = ___ x ___ = ___ kg·m/s) is related to the ball's ___ in momentum, which connects to the idea that momentum is ___ between objects during interactions.

lessons.title: Impulse and the Impulse-Momentum Theorem
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can calculate impulse as force multiplied by time, apply the impulse-momentum theorem (J = Delta p), and explain how increasing collision time decreases the force experienced.
lessons.circle_prompt: Would you rather fall onto concrete or a mattress? Jump from a height and land stiff-legged or bend your knees? Why? What is your body doing differently in each case?
lessons.do_now: A 0.5 kg ball drops and hits the ground, changing its velocity from -5 m/s to +3 m/s in 0.02 seconds. What is the change in momentum? What average force did the ground exert on the ball?
materials: Various padding materials (bubble wrap, foam, towels, newspaper)
Containers for egg drop (cups, bags, boxes)

engage.description: Teacher demonstration: Drop an egg onto a hard surface (it breaks). Then drop an identical egg from the same height onto a thick foam pad (it survives). Ask: Both eggs experienced the same change in momentum (same mass, same velocity change). So why did one break and the other didn't? The difference must be in the FORCE — which depends on the TIME of the collision.

explore.description: Engineering challenge: Groups design a container using provided padding materials that will protect an egg dropped from 2 m. Before dropping, each group must calculate: (a) the egg's velocity at impact (using free fall), (b) the change in momentum, and (c) the average force if the collision time is 0.01 s (no padding) vs. 0.1 s (with padding). After predictions, groups test their designs.

explain.description: Define impulse: J = F * Delta t (force x time), measured in N·s. State the Impulse-Momentum Theorem: J = Delta p, meaning F * Delta t = m * Delta v. Key insight: for a given change in momentum, increasing the collision time DECREASES the force: F = Delta p / Delta t. Show the graphical interpretation: impulse is the area under a Force-time graph. Work through an airbag calculation: same Delta p, but airbag extends time from 0.005 s to 0.05 s.

elaborate.description: Real-world applications analysis: Students explain the physics behind: (1) Why cars have crumple zones. (2) Why boxers roll with punches. (3) Why gymnasts bend their knees on landing. (4) Why there are padded walls behind the goals in ice hockey. For each, students identify what changes (time), what stays the same (impulse/momentum change), and what decreases (force).

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A 60 kg person jumps from a 1.0 m ledge. (a) Calculate their velocity just before hitting the ground. (b) Calculate the impulse needed to stop them. (c) If they land stiff-legged (Delta t = 0.01 s), what is the average force? (d) If they bend their knees (Delta t = 0.3 s), what is the average force?

differentiation.approaching: Provide the Impulse-Momentum Theorem as a visual equation chain: F x t = m x Delta v. Include a 'big time = small force' diagram showing the inverse relationship. Pre-calculate the egg's impact velocity for the engineering challenge.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the egg drop engineering challenge and impulse calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Analyze a Force-time graph with non-constant force (triangular or parabolic shape) and calculate impulse as the area under the curve. Compare impulse from an airbag Force-time graph to a rigid steering wheel graph.
differentiation.ell: Use the egg drop as primary instruction — the physical experience makes the abstract concept concrete. Provide a visual impulse-momentum chain: 'Larger time → Smaller force → Less damage.' Include bilingual vocabulary.
differentiation.iep: Provide the impulse formula on a reference card. Focus on the conceptual relationship (longer time = less force) before calculations. Break the exit ticket into two separate problems. Allow calculator use throughout.

lessons.crse_connection: Explore the physics of traditional martial arts techniques — karate practitioners break boards by maximizing force (short contact time), while aikido practitioners redirect an opponent's momentum over a longer time to reduce injury. Connect to how these cultural practices from Japan and East Asia embody impulse-momentum physics.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'impulse': An airbag reduces injury during a crash because___. Both a padded and unpadded dashboard produce the same impulse, but the padded dashboard is safer because___. The gymnast bends her knees on landing, so the force on her legs is___.

vocabulary.definition: The product of force and the time interval over which it acts; J = F * Delta t; measured in N·s; equal to the change in momentum
The impulse on an object equals its change in momentum: F * Delta t = m * Delta v = Delta p
The duration of contact between colliding objects; increasing collision time decreases the average force for the same momentum change
A section of a vehicle designed to deform during a collision, increasing the collision time and reducing the force transferred to passengers
A graph showing force on the y-axis and time on the x-axis; the area under the curve equals the impulse

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Impulse — Force Times Time
Section 2: The Impulse-Momentum Theorem — J = Delta p
Section 3: The Inverse Relationship Between Force and Time
Section 4: Real-World Safety Applications — Airbags, Crumple Zones, Padding
Section 5: Impulse from a Force-Time Graph

cer.phenomenon: Two identical crash test dummies in identical cars hit a wall at 50 km/h (13.9 m/s). Car A has a rigid steel frame and comes to a stop in 0.05 s. Car B has engineered crumple zones and comes to a stop in 0.5 s. Both drivers have a mass of 75 kg. The dummy in Car A experiences severe 'injuries' while the dummy in Car B survives with minor damage.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the impulse-momentum theorem, I claim that the crumple zone reduces the peak force by a factor of approximately ___ because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the impulse (change in momentum) for both dummies — it is the same. Then calculate the average force in each car using F = Delta p / Delta t.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because both dummies experience the same impulse of ___ N·s (since Delta p = m * Delta v = ___), but Car A's force is ___ N while Car B's force is only ___ N. The crumple zone increased the collision time by a factor of ___, which reduced the force by the same factor because ___.

lessons.title: Conservation of Momentum
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can apply the law of conservation of momentum to calculate unknown velocities before or after a collision in an isolated system.
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever played pool or billiards? What happens when the cue ball hits another ball straight on? What about at an angle? Is anything 'lost' in the collision?
lessons.do_now: A 2 kg cart moving at 3 m/s collides with a stationary 1 kg cart. After the collision, the 2 kg cart moves at 1 m/s in the same direction. What is the velocity of the 1 kg cart after the collision? (Hint: total momentum before = total momentum after.)
materials: Dynamics carts with spring bumpers (2 per group)

engage.description: Show a Newton's cradle in action. Ask: When one ball swings in and hits, why does exactly one ball swing out the other side? Why not two balls at half the speed? Students predict and discuss. Introduce the idea that something is conserved — total momentum of the system does not change if no external forces act.

explore.description: Lab investigation: Groups perform cart collisions on a dynamics track. They measure velocities before and after collision (using photogates or distance/time). Trial 1: equal mass carts, one at rest. Trial 2: unequal mass carts, one at rest. Trial 3: both carts moving toward each other. For each trial, students calculate total momentum before and after and compare.

explain.description: State the Law of Conservation of Momentum: In an isolated system (no external net force), total momentum before an interaction equals total momentum after. Mathematical form: m1v1i + m2v2i = m1v1f + m2v2f. Derive from Newton's Third Law: during the collision, F_12 = -F_21, so Delta p_1 = -Delta p_2, meaning the total change in momentum is zero. Work through two examples: a collision where both objects are initially moving, and an explosion (person throwing a ball).

elaborate.description: Recoil problem: A 60 kg astronaut floating at rest in space throws a 5 kg toolbox at 3 m/s away from the space station. What is the astronaut's velocity after the throw? Students apply conservation of momentum with initial momentum = 0 and recognize this is the same physics as rocket propulsion.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A 10 kg bowling ball moving at 6 m/s strikes a 1.5 kg pin at rest. After the collision, the bowling ball moves at 5.2 m/s in the same direction. (a) What is the total momentum before the collision? (b) What is the pin's velocity after the collision? (c) Is momentum conserved? Show your work.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a conservation of momentum equation template with labeled slots: m1*v1i + m2*v2i = m1*v1f + m2*v2f. Include a checklist: 'Is one object at rest? Set that v = 0. Are they moving in opposite directions? Make one velocity negative.' Walk through one worked example before independent practice.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the collision lab and conservation of momentum calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Analyze a multi-object collision (three objects) and verify conservation of momentum. Calculate the percentage of kinetic energy lost in each lab trial to classify the collision type (preview of elastic/inelastic).
differentiation.ell: Use the physical cart collisions as primary instruction. Provide a visual before/after diagram template where students draw and label velocities. Include bilingual vocabulary and a labeled equation template.
differentiation.iep: Provide the conservation equation on a reference card with an example. Pre-fill 'before' values in the equation and let students solve for the unknown 'after' value. Reduce to two-object, one-at-rest problems only. Allow calculator use.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the physics of car collisions and how conservation of momentum is used in accident reconstruction — a field that intersects with social justice when determining fault in crashes. Highlight how bias in accident investigations has historically affected communities of color and how objective physics-based reconstruction can promote fairness.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'conservation of momentum': Total momentum is conserved in a collision because___. The bowling ball slows down after hitting the pin, but the total momentum of the system doesn't change because___. The astronaut was initially at rest and threw the toolbox forward, so the astronaut must move___.

vocabulary.definition: In an isolated system with no external net force, the total momentum before an interaction equals the total momentum after
A system in which no external net forces act; only internal forces between objects within the system are present
Forces between objects within the system (e.g., collision forces, explosion forces); these cannot change the total momentum of the system
Forces from outside the system (e.g., friction with the ground, gravity if not accounted for); these CAN change the total momentum
The backward motion of one object when another is propelled forward; an application of conservation of momentum starting from rest

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: The Law of Conservation of Momentum
Section 2: Deriving Conservation from Newton's Third Law
Section 3: Applying the Conservation Equation to Collisions
Section 4: Explosions and Recoil — Momentum Starts at Zero
Section 5: When Is Momentum NOT Conserved? — The Role of External Forces

cer.phenomenon: In a football game, a 100 kg linebacker running east at 5 m/s tackles a 80 kg running back moving east at 7 m/s. After the tackle, both players move together (they stick together). A referee flags the play and claims the running back was moving forward before the tackle.
cer.claim_starter: Based on conservation of momentum, I claim that after the tackle, both players move ___ at ___ m/s because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the total momentum before the collision (both moving east, so add). Use m1v1i + m2v2i = (m1 + m2)vf to find the final velocity.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because the total momentum before is ___ + ___ = ___ kg·m/s eastward. Since they stick together, vf = ___/(___ + ___) = ___ m/s eastward. The positive (eastward) direction confirms the running back's forward motion was sufficient to carry both players ___.

lessons.title: Elastic and Inelastic Collisions
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can classify collisions as elastic, inelastic, or perfectly inelastic and determine whether kinetic energy is conserved in each type.
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about different types of collisions you have seen — a bouncy ball vs. a lump of clay, bumper cars vs. a car crash. What is different about each? Does anything get 'used up' in some collisions?
lessons.do_now: Two 1 kg carts collide on a frictionless track. Before: Cart A moves at 4 m/s, Cart B is at rest. After: Cart A is at rest, Cart B moves at 4 m/s. Calculate the total kinetic energy before and after. Was kinetic energy conserved?
materials: Dynamics carts with magnetic bumpers (elastic) and Velcro bumpers (inelastic)
Happy ball and sad ball (same size, different bounce)

engage.description: Drop a 'happy ball' (bouncy) and a 'sad ball' (non-bouncy, same size and appearance) from the same height. The happy ball bounces high while the sad ball barely bounces. Ask: Both had the same momentum change (from moving down to stopping). But one bounces and one doesn't. What's different? Where did the energy go in the sad ball? Introduce the idea that momentum is always conserved, but kinetic energy may not be.

explore.description: Groups perform two types of collisions on the dynamics track: (1) Magnetic bumper carts (elastic-like — they bounce apart) and (2) Velcro bumper carts (perfectly inelastic — they stick together). For each, students measure velocities before and after, calculate total momentum (should be conserved in both), and calculate total kinetic energy before and after (conserved only in elastic).

explain.description: Define three collision types: (1) Perfectly elastic — objects bounce apart, both momentum and KE conserved (ideal case: billiard balls). (2) Inelastic — objects separate but KE is not conserved; some KE converts to heat, sound, deformation. (3) Perfectly inelastic — objects stick together; maximum KE loss (but momentum still conserved). Key formula for perfectly inelastic: m1v1i + m2v2i = (m1 + m2)vf. For elastic collisions between equal masses with one at rest: objects exchange velocities.

elaborate.description: Problem: A 1500 kg car traveling at 20 m/s rear-ends a 1000 kg car at rest. (a) If they stick together (perfectly inelastic), find the final velocity. (b) Calculate KE before and after. (c) What percentage of KE was lost? (d) Where did the lost energy go? (heat, sound, deformation of the metal)

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: Two objects collide. Object A (3 kg) moves at 5 m/s east. Object B (2 kg) moves at 3 m/s west. They stick together. (a) Find the final velocity. (b) Is this elastic or inelastic? (c) Calculate the KE lost.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a collision type comparison chart: Elastic (bounce, KE conserved), Inelastic (separate, KE not conserved), Perfectly Inelastic (stick, max KE loss). Include worked examples for each type.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the collision lab comparing elastic and inelastic collisions and solve both types of problems.
differentiation.advanced: Solve a fully elastic collision algebraically (two equations: conservation of momentum and conservation of KE) to find both final velocities. Analyze the percentage of energy lost as a function of mass ratio in perfectly inelastic collisions.
differentiation.ell: Use the physical cart demonstrations as primary instruction. Provide a visual collision comparison poster with arrows and labels. Color-code: green = elastic (all KE kept), red = perfectly inelastic (max KE lost). Include bilingual vocabulary.
differentiation.iep: Focus on perfectly inelastic collisions only (stick together — one equation, one unknown). Provide the combined formula on a reference card. Break KE calculations into single steps. Allow calculator use throughout.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how collision physics is used in car safety ratings by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and how access to safer vehicles is an equity issue — families in lower-income communities often drive older cars with fewer safety features. Connect to how physics knowledge empowers consumers to make informed safety decisions.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'elastic' and 'inelastic': In a perfectly inelastic collision, the objects stick together, so the final velocity is found by___. Momentum is conserved in all collisions, but kinetic energy is only conserved in ___ collisions because___. The sad ball lost most of its kinetic energy on impact because___.

vocabulary.definition: A collision in which both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved; objects bounce apart with no permanent deformation
A collision in which momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not; some KE is converted to heat, sound, or deformation
A collision in which the objects stick together after impact; momentum is conserved but the maximum amount of kinetic energy is lost
The energy of motion; KE = 1/2 mv^2; measured in Joules (J)
A permanent change in shape resulting from a collision; represents energy transferred from kinetic energy to internal energy

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Three Types of Collisions — Elastic, Inelastic, Perfectly Inelastic
Section 2: Momentum Is ALWAYS Conserved (in isolated systems)
Section 3: Kinetic Energy — Sometimes Conserved, Sometimes Not
Section 4: Perfectly Inelastic Collisions — Objects Stick Together
